WHO WE ARE
IEX is India’s premier electricity exchange providing a nationwide, automated trading platform 
for physical delivery of electricity, renewable energy and certificates including renewable energy 
certificates as well as energy saving certificates. The exchange platform enables efficient price 
discovery and increases accessibility and transparency of the energy market in India, while 
also enhancing the speed and efficiency of trade execution. The Exchange is ISO Certified for 
Quality Management, Information Security Management and Environment Management since 
August 2016. Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) is a publicly listed company with NSE and BSE since 
October 2017 and is approved and regulated by Central Electricity Regulatory Commission since 
27 June 2008.

A RESILIENT AND FUTURE-READY POWER SECTOR
Electricity is one of the key enablers of India’s economic transformation. As the nation 
advances towards becoming a global manufacturing and digital powerhouse, the power 
sector continues to evolve with greater scale, reliability and technological integration. 
Over the past decade, the country’s power sector 
ecosystem has undergone remarkable transition - from 
addressing shortages and expanding access to building 
a modern, resilient and future-ready energy infrastructure 
- capable of supporting sustained economic growth. 
India’s power demand trajectory reflects the pace 
of the country’s development. Rapid urbanisation, 
rising industrial activity, infrastructure expansion and 
increasing digital adoption are continuously driving 
electricity consumption upward. During FY’26, India 
successfully met a peak power demand of 245 GW while 
reducing power shortages to just 0.03%, which marks 
a substantial improvement from 4.2% in FY’14. This 
transformation highlights the strengthening generation 
capacity, transmission networks and grid management 
systems across the country.
One of the most significant achievements of the sector 
has been the expansion of electricity access across 
India.  The world’s largest synchronous national grid now 
exceeds 5 lakh circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission 
lines. Through large-scale rural electrification and last-
mile connectivity initiatives, electricity today reaches 
nearly every village and household in the country. Flagship 
programmes such as Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti 
Yojana (DDUGJY), Integrated Power Development Scheme 
(IPDS) and Saubhagya accelerated the creation of modern 
distribution infrastructure and enabled electricity access 
for nearly 30 million households. Improved supply 
reliability has positively impacted education, healthcare, 
agriculture and small enterprises, particularly in rural and 
semi-urban India.
The sector’s evolution is also visible in the steady 
improvement in quality and availability of power supply. 
Average daily power supply in rural India has increased 
substantially over the last decade, while urban areas 
continue to witness near-round-the-clock availability. 
Per capita electricity consumption in India has also 
risen to 1,460 kilowatt-hours in FY’25, registering an

the country’s renewable energy ecosystem and its ability 
to integrate clean energy into the national grid.
Continued investments in transmission infrastructure 
are ensuring that growing renewable capacity can be 
efficiently integrated and delivered across regions. The 
National Electricity Plan 2023–2032 outlines a strong 
roadmap for future-ready transmission systems, inter-
regional connectivity and grid expansion to support rising 
electricity demand and emerging energy applications.
The financial and operational performance of distribution 
utilities has also shown notable improvement. AT&C 
losses declined to 15% in FY’25 from 16% in FY’24, while 
the narrowing of the ACS-ARR gap and improved payment 
discipline across the value chain reflect the impact 
of sustained reforms and operational strengthening. 
Timely payments to generators and a growing focus on 
power procurement optimisation further underscore the 
sector’s transition towards greater financial discipline 
and operational efficiency. These developments are 
creating a healthier and more sustainable ecosystem for 
long-term sectoral growth.
As India’s economy continues to expand, electricity 
will remain central to industrial competitiveness, digital 
growth, urban development and sustainability ambitions. 
Emerging sectors such as electric mobility, data centres, 
green hydrogen and advanced manufacturing are 
expected to further accelerate demand for reliable and 
clean power.
In this evolving landscape, the Indian Energy Exchange 
(IEX) endeavors to remain at the forefront of technology-
enabled and market-driven solutions in ensuring 
efficiency, flexibility and transparency across the 
power ecosystem. India’s power sector today is not 
only supporting economic growth but also building 
the foundation for a more connected, sustainable and 
energy-secure future.

THE SHIFT TO SMARTER POWER PROCUREMENT
State power utilities in the country are steadily transforming how they procure electricity 
and the shift is already evident in the numbers. Across India, distribution companies 
are moving beyond traditional methods and involving power exchanges into their core 
supply planning processes. What was once an option to address short-term deficits 
or unexpected demand has evolved into a strategic procurement channel, guided by 
data-driven decision-making. On the strength of leveraging price signals, generation 
economics, and time-of-day demand patterns, utilities are adopting a more dynamic 
and informed approach to sourcing power.
This transformation is reshaping three critical elements 
of DISCOM operations: the timing of procurement 
decisions, the scheduling of State-allocated generation, 
and the daily optimisation of supply-demand balance. 
States such as Uttarakhand, West Bengal, and Punjab 
exemplify this shift, having embedded market-based 
procurement as a central pillar of their operational 
strategy.
In Punjab, for instance, long-term PPAs had kept the 
load curve largely flat, but the State discom has shifted 
significant demand to daytime hours to tap surplus, low-
cost solar power. By actively tracking price trends and 
increasing participation in DAM, RTM, and the Green 
Day-Ahead Market on IEX, the State discom optimized 
costs, improved reliability, and supported sustainability 
goals, all reflected in a 50% CAGR in exchange purchases

over five years. Once a seasonal buyer during the paddy 
season, Punjab now engages year-round by monitoring 
market signals and weather patterns. In FY’26, heavy 
rainfall reduced paddy-season demand across the 
State, enabling the State discom to sell surplus power 
on exchanges to the quantum of over 1 BU — unlocking 
new revenue while maintaining grid security and 
avoiding DSM penalties. This strategy of buying smartly 
and selling surplus positioned the State as a leader in 
market-based procurement and it also became the first 
government entity to acquire a private thermal plant, 
enhancing supply and liquidity.
Similarly, in West Bengal, which operates under different 
demand conditions, the State discom leveraged 
competitive exchange prices through a data-driven 
strategy. In FY’26, it procured nearly 7 BU from power 
exchanges, an increase of about 250% YoY, even as 
peak demand rose just 2%. By optimizing purchases at 
an average cost of nearly `3/unit, the State achieved 
significant savings. The discom’s strategy was to 
maximise low-cost solar hours on DAM and RTM, 
where average prices touched `2.34/unit and `2.51/
unit, respectively. Instead of running higher-cost thermal 
plants at full load, West Bengal operated them at technical 
minimum and met additional demand via cheaper 
exchange power. This reduced fuel use, cut costs, and 
enabled greater integration of renewable energy.
Uttarakhand has also integrated power exchanges into 
routine supply planning, using data-driven procurement 
and saved over `160 crore in FY’26, while also earning 
`125 crore from REC sales. Initially procuring via the 
DEEP (Discovery of Efficient Electricity Price) portal, the 
State discom shifted to a diversified strategy leveraging 
exchange products to lower costs. It sourced nearly 
850 MUs through long-duration contracts at about 
`3.59/unit and saved `160 crore overall. As a hydro-rich 
State, Uttarakhand generates surplus renewable energy 
beyond its RPO needs which it monetized by selling 35 
lakh RECs on exchanges at an average price of `350 per 
REC, generating `125 crore in additional revenue.
Power procurement trends from Telangana discoms 
also reveal market-based dynamic sourcing as a core 
operational strategy. Improved supply from renewables 
(solar, hydro, wind) alongside steady coal generation 
softened prices enabling discoms to replace costlier 
power with exchange-based procurement. Telangana 
capitalized on this opportunity through a data-driven 
approach. In FY’26, the State discoms procured about 13 
BU from exchanges at an average of `3.04/unit, saving 
around `700 crore.
The growing reliance on exchanges across States 
signals a lasting change in procurement strategy. Data 
from multiple regions shows measurable gains: lower 
purchase costs, better demand–supply balance and 
new revenue streams from surplus power. As renewable 
capacity continues to expand and hourly price variation 
becomes sharper, States that actively respond to market 
signals are likely to widen their financial advantage. 
Exchange-led procurement is therefore not just a short-
term tactic, it is becoming a defining feature of how 
India’s power system is planned and managed.

GREEN MARKETS: TECHNOLOGY ENABLING A 
SUSTAINABLE ENERGY FUTURE
India’s energy transition is no longer a vision for the future, it is a transition unfolding at a 
rapid pace. With non-fossil sources accounting for half of the country’s installed power 
capacity, the nation has entered a defining decade in its journey towards achieving its 
2030 climate commitments and 2070 commitment of net-zero emissions. Renewable 
energy has moved beyond incremental growth to become a fundamental pillar of India’s 
power system, delivering lower energy costs, reducing dependence on imported fuels, 
and reshaping electricity markets. 
As this transition gathers momentum, the challenge is 
no longer limited to adding renewable capacity. The next 
phase lies in integrating renewable energy efficiently 
into the grid. The growing share of solar and wind 
generation has introduced a new level of complexity to 
system operations. Their inherent variability has led to 
larger intra-day forecast deviations, sharper net-load 
ramps and more frequent real-time imbalances, making 
flexibility and responsive market mechanisms essential 
for maintaining grid reliability.
At IEX, we believe that well-designed markets are central 
to enabling this transformation. Over the years, we 
have continuously expanded our market architecture 
to address the evolving needs of India’s power sector, 
creating innovative products that enhance flexibility, 
improve price discovery and accelerate renewable 
energy adoption.
A significant milestone in this journey has been the 
creation of India’s first Green Market through the Green 
Day-Ahead Market (G-DAM) and the Green Term-Ahead 
Market (G-TAM). IEX has built transparent, market-
based avenues for energy procurement and trading. 
These products empower renewable-rich States to 
monetise surplus green power beyond their compliance 
obligations while enabling generators to adopt flexible 
procurement strategies, ranging from hybrid market-
PPA structures to fully market-based models. In doing 
so, IEX is strengthening the economic case for renewable 
energy while supporting the sustainability ambitions of 
both corporates and the nation at large.

The market response has been equally encouraging. As 
renewable generation has increased, green power prices 
have become increasingly competitive, encouraging 
greater participation in the Green Market. This has 
translated into strong growth in traded volumes across 
the Green Market, registering 23% YoY growth, with the 
Green Market accounting for nearly 8% of the electricity 
volume traded on the Exchange in FY’26. The increasing 
contribution of green market products to IEX’s overall 
product mix reflects the growing confidence of market 
participants in transparent, exchange-based renewable 
power procurement.
Alongside the Green Market, the Real-Time Market (RTM) 
has emerged as an indispensable pillar of renewable 
integration. As renewable penetration increases, balancing 
demand and supply closer to delivery has become critical.

segments of the energy value chain.

foundation of technology, innovation and customer centricity.

innovation and customer focused solutions, the Exchange

participants while strengthening its position as India’s leading 
electricity marketplace. This commitment to innovation and 
operational excellence has enabled IEX to remain agile in 
a rapidly evolving energy landscape. As the organisation

and scaling India’s largest electricity exchange, encompassing

long term value.

across every major energy commodity. Electricity, natural gas, 
carbon and coal each have a distinct role to play in strengthening 
energy security, supporting industrial growth and enabling the 
country’s transition to a lower-carbon future.

creating specialised exchanges designed to meet the unique 
requirements of each market while remaining anchored in 
the same core principles of transparency, efficiency and

bringing market-based solutions to another critical pillar of 
India’s energy economy. 
Together, these initiatives reflect IEX’s commitment to building 
the market infrastructure needed to support India’s evolving 
energy landscape.

IGX – INDIA’S FIRST AND ONLY 
AUTHORIZED NATIONAL LEVEL PHYSICAL

FY’26 marked an important milestone for the Indian Gas 
Exchange (“IGX”) as IGX’s electronic exchange platform 
(“Exchange”) completed five years of operations. Since its 
launch in 2020, IGX has facilitated in bringing transparency, 
efficiency and market-based price discovery to India’s natural 
gas sector. IGX has over last five years, established itself as an 
organized, transparent and technology-enabled marketplace 
for physical delivery of natural gas, facilitating participation 
from stakeholders including the gas producers, gas marketing 
companies, city gas distribution companies, power generation 
companies, refineries, fertilizer companies, terminal operators 
and industrial consumers. 
Natural gas and LNG have progressively solidified their position 
as critical pillars and have become the fundamental elements 
of the global energy landscape, functioning both as a versatile 
fossil fuel and as a strategic bridge in the transition toward 
lower-carbon energy systems 
The city gas distribution sector is expected to remain a key driver 
of natural gas demand growth in India, supported by ongoing 
expansion of infrastructure, increasing urbanization and fuel-
switching initiatives. IGX provides a transparent and organized 
platform that enables efficient trading of gas and supports the 
development of a market-driven gas ecosystem.
GROWING SCALE AND MARKET RELEVANCE
Since IGX commenced operations, the Exchange has witnessed 
significant growth in trading activity, with cumulative traded 
volumes of 76.79, 60.02 and 40.84 million Metric Million 
British Thermal Units (“million MMBtu”) in Fiscals 2026, 2025 
and 2024, respectively, growing at a CAGR of 37.12% between 
Fiscals 2024 and 2026. Monthly contracts are the undisputed 
backbone of IGX volumes, accounting for approximately 64% 
of the total Fiscal 2026 volumes. While monthly contracts lead, 
fortnightly and weekly contracts show significant traction.
Gas Index of India (“GIXI”), the Exchange’s flagship price index, 
continues to serve as a transparent, nationwide benchmark 
reflecting spot gas prices across delivery points, regions and 
the market as a whole for market participants. 
With this performance, IGX facilitated close to 2.82% of India’s 
total gas consumption in FY’26. As of FY’26, the Exchange’s 
platform comprised trading across 19 delivery points spanning 
five regional hubs and 10 contract types across the spot and 
forward markets.
During FY’26, IGX recorded a profit after tax of `418.68 million, 
registering a growth in profit after tax of 35.29% over the 
previous year. 
NEW CONTRACTS
During the year, the Exchange launched the Balance of Month 
(BoM) Contract, enabling market participants to procure or sell 
gas for the remaining days of an ongoing calendar month. This 
new offering complements IGX’s existing portfolio of spot and 
forward contracts and provides additional flexibility for short-
term gas procurement and risk management.
NEW DELIVERY POINTS
To further enhance physical market accessibility, IGX expanded 
its delivery options with the addition of the Palanpur delivery 
point during FY’26 strengthening connectivity between the 
Gujarat gas grid and demand centres in the Western and 
Northern regions. As of FY’26, IGX’s delivery framework 
comprised 19 delivery points across [five regional hubs - 
Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western and Central, spanning 
LNG terminals, pipeline intersection points and domestic gas 
fields. The continued expansion and diversification of delivery 
infrastructure strengthen market connectivity and provides 
participants with flexibility in procuring natural gas across 
regions.

India’s natural gas market is expected to benefit from ongoing 
regulatory and policy initiatives aimed at enhancing market 
efficiency, improving infrastructure utilization and facilitating 
exchange-based gas trading. The PNGRB’s unified tariff 
framework (UFT), effective January 1, 2026, replaced the 
earlier 3-zone with a simplified 2-zone regime, reducing the 
cost of transporting gas across the national grid and improving 
pan-India arbitrage opportunities. The Oilfields (Regulation 
and Development) Amendment Act, 2025, which came into 
force on April 15, 2025, modernized the regulatory framework 
governing upstream oil and gas operations with the objective 
of accelerating domestic exploration and production. The 
PNGRB also proposed further reforms under the Petroleum 
and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (Access Code for Common 
Carrier or Contract Carrier Natural Gas Pipelines) Regulations, 
including a more transparent, flexible and consumer friendly 
capacity booking framework, including online, 24x7 capacity 
booking and booking on intraday and day-ahead basis and 
the establishment of an Independent System Operator (ISO). 
Collectively, these reforms are expected to enhance liquidity, 
improve price discovery and support the development of a 
more competitive and vibrant gas trading ecosystem in India.
These developments, together with continued expansion of the 
national gas pipeline grid and city gas distribution network, and 
the GOI’s stated objective of raising the share of natural gas in 
India’s primary energy mix from approximately 7% to 15% by 
2030, are expected to support the broader transition toward 
cleaner, more efficient and more flexible energy systems. During 
the year, the natural gas market was also affected by geopolitical 
uncertainty, particularly disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, 
which tightened global supply and drove sharp price volatility. 
As imported regasified LNG (RLNG) constituted a substantial 
share of gas traded on the Exchange, these disruptions 
together with elevated prices and the policy response under 
the Natural Gas (Supply Regulation) Order, 2026 contributed to 
a decline in RLNG trading volumes towards the end of FY’26, 
which subsequently recovered. Such geopolitical developments 
influence LNG availability, trading volumes and price discovery 
underscoring the importance of supply diversification and 
continued development of domestic gas sources for the long-
term resilience of India’s gas market.
Having completed five years of operations, IGX enters its 
next phase to expand trading volumes and liquidity across 
its exchange platform, capitalize on expected growth in the 
organized market for natural gas, expand its product offering, 
develop new gas market platforms and adjacent trading 
segments, continue its regulatory and policy advocacy to 
deepen the natural gas market in India, leverage its partnerships 
to develop derivatives and financial market integration and to 
invest in and expand IGX Academy to create awareness on gas 
exchange fundamentals.

ICX: BUILDING THE FOUNDATION FOR 
INDIA’S CLEAN ENERGY MARKETS
As India’s clean energy transition gathers pace, businesses are 
increasingly looking for credible and globally accepted ways 
to demonstrate their use of renewable electricity and advance 
their sustainability commitments. This growing need has 
accelerated the adoption of market-based instruments that 
bring transparency, credibility and international recognition to 
renewable energy consumption.
Recognising this opportunity, ICX the wholly owned subsidiary 
of IEX, took a pioneering step by bringing the globally recognized 
International 
Renewable 
Energy 
Certificates 
(I-REC(E)) 
framework to India. Accredited by the I-Track Foundation as the 
Local Issuer on 2nd September 2024, ICX has since emerged as 
a crucial enabler for corporates seeking to credibly demonstrate 
their renewable energy usage in line with international standards.
WHAT IS I-REC(E)?
The International Renewable Energy Certificate for Electricity 
[I-REC(E)] is a tradable Energy Attribute Certificate (EAC) 
that conveys verified information about the production 
of one megawatt-hour (1 MWh) of electricity such as its 
source, production facility, and its capacity. Accredited by the 
International Tracking Standard Foundation, I-REC(E) enables 
electricity users worldwide to credibly report renewable 
consumption for Scope 2 emissions, sustainability disclosures, 
and voluntary initiatives. By procuring I-REC(E), companies 
can claim renewable energy usage, reduce Scope 2 emissions, 
and align with leading global frameworks such as RE100 and 
the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)—demonstrating 
measurable progress toward net-zero and sustainability goals.
STRENGTHENING TRUST AND INTEGRITY
Building on IEX’s deep expertise in the Indian power sector, ICX 
has brought strong governance and credibility to the voluntary 
I-REC(E) market by tailoring international frameworks to India’s 
regulatory environment. Aligned with the I-TRACK standards 
and the I-REC(E) Code, ICX has instituted rigorous processes 
to ensure integrity, transparency, and the elimination of double 
counting. This includes conducting detailed analyses of Central 
and State regulations, embedding regulatory checks into device 
registration and certificate issuance, and proactively addressing 
challenges related to Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPOs). 
Additionally, ICX has streamlined the identification and 
treatment of banking quantum as per State-specific rules, 
ensuring robust compliance. Through these measures, ICX has 
added substantial value as the local I-REC(E) Issuer, fostering 
trust and confidence for corporates and stakeholders in India’s 
renewable energy certificate ecosystem. This has resulted in 
major shifts in the device (power plant) registration and I-REC(E) 
issuance processes leading to increased confidence among 
market participants and the product’s market value. The impact 
of this initiative is already being felt on the ground. By enabling 
access to I-REC(E), ICX has provided Indian corporates with 
the same credibility and recognition enjoyed by their peers 
globally. This international parity has not only strengthened 
ESG disclosures but also enhanced investor confidence in the 
country’s corporate sustainability journey.

in new renewable energy facility registrations, increasing from 
411 facilities in FY’25 to 614 facilities in FY’26. The continued 
growth reflects increasing participation from renewable 
energy generators and rising demand from corporates seeking 
credible solutions for Scope 2 emissions reduction and globally 
recognised sustainability reporting.
EXPANDING IEX’S DIVERSIFICATION 
JOURNEY
The development of India’s I-REC(E) market represents an 
important milestone in the diversification journey of IEX. By 
extending its market expertise beyond electricity and natural gas 
into environmental products, ICX is creating new opportunities 
for market-based climate solutions while supporting India’s 
broader clean energy ambitions. As renewable energy 
capacity continues to expand and sustainability commitments 
become increasingly central to corporate strategy, ICX is well 
positioned to deepen the adoption of I-REC(E), broaden market 
participation and strengthen India’s clean energy market 
ecosystem. Through this initiative, ICX is enabling businesses 
to seamlessly align with global sustainability frameworks while 
contributing to the country’s long-term energy transition.
INDIAN COAL EXCHANGE: BUILDING THE 
MARKET ARCHITECTURE FOR INDIA’S COAL 
ECONOMY
Earlier in 2026, IEX incorporated Indian Coal Exchange to 
support the next phase of India’s Coal Economy.
For decades, India’s coal sector is focused on increasing 
domestic production to meet the country’s growing energy 
demand. Today, the challenge is evolving to ensure that coal 
production is discovered, priced, traded and allocated more 
efficiently. India produced a little over 1.0 billion tonnes of coal 
in FY’26 and production is expected to reach 1.5 billion tonnes 
by FY’30 and 1.8 billion tonnes by FY’35. While coal’s share in 
power generation is projected to decline from 71% in FY’26 to 
50% by FY’35, absolute share of coal in Indian energy mix shall 
continue to grow. This is supported by the fact that, production 
from captive and commercial mines crossed 200 million tonnes 
for the first time in FY’26 and is projected to reach 500 million 
tonnes by FY’35.  
This marks a structural shift in India’s coal market. As 
supply expands and market participants increase, efficiency, 
transparency and price discovery are becoming as important as 
production itself. Recognising this transition, IEX incorporated 
the Indian Coal Exchange Limited, extending its expertise in 
building transparent and efficient marketplaces to India’s coal 
sector.
CREATING A MARKET FOR A MULTI-SELLER 
COAL ECONOMY
Policy reforms over the past few years have transformed the 
structure of the coal market. Commercial coal mining has 
removed the end use restrictions encouraging wider private 
participation. While captive mines were permitted to sell up to 
50% of their production in the open market. Consequently, Coal 
India’s share of domestic production has declined from around 
80% in FY’22 to 74% in FY’26, while captive and commercial 
mines now contribute 20% and SCCL accounts for 6%. 
Although Coal India sold around 11% of its production through 
e-auctions in FY’26, a significant share of surplus coal from 
captive and commercial mines continues to be traded through 
bilateral arrangements. As tradable volumes increase, a multi-
seller market requires transparent price discovery, standardised 
contracts and efficient mechanisms for matching buyers and 
sellers.
LAYING THE FOUNDATION FOR EFFICIENT 
COAL MARKETS
The notification of the Coal Exchange Rules, 2026, following 
amendments to the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, has established the regulatory framework for 
exchange-based coal trading.
The Indian Coal Exchange has the potential to create 
transparent domestic benchmark prices, improve procurement 
efficiency and strengthen market visibility across the coal value 
chain. Beyond facilitating transactions, it can support better 
allocation of domestic coal, improve market competitiveness 
and contribute to more efficient utilisation of the country’s 
growing coal resources.
The incorporation of the Indian Coal Exchange reflects IEX’s 
commitment to building the market infrastructure needed for 
India’s evolving energy landscape. As the coal sector becomes 
larger, more competitive and increasingly market-driven, IEX 
is poised to support the next phase of India’s coal economy 
through greater transparency, efficiency and robust price 
discovery.

POWER SECTOR: STRENGTHENING FROM WITHIN
India’s power sector in FY’26 entered an important new phase, 
one where efficiency, flexibility, and access became as important 
as demand growth itself. At 1,708 billion units, overall electricity 
consumption remained largely stable year-on-year, influenced 
by an extended monsoon season and milder summers. Even 
so, the sector made measurable and meaningful progress in 
capacity creation, supply conditions, and market participation, 
providing a clear signal that the system is strengthening 
structurally.
The year witnessed a record incremental capacity addition

India’s total installed capacity to 533 GW. Of this, renewable 
energy now accounts for over 50% at 275 GW, making India 
the world’s third largest in renewable capacity. In fact, India 
achieved this milestone five years ahead of its 2030 target

competitive prices.
Fuel availability in FY’26 further bolstered market stability. 
Domestic coal production crossed one billion tonnes, while coal 
inventories remained at a comfortable 25 days. This favourable 
fuel supply environment enhanced supply side liquidity on the 
exchange platform, leading to a competitive price discovery.
The average DAM price in FY’26 stood at `3.86/unit, lower 
by 14% compared with FY’25. This translated into a power 
procurement advantage for DISCOMs and C&I consumers.

IEX BUSINESS PERFORMANCE: A YEAR OF ROBUST GROWTH
IEX delivered a strong performance in FY’26, with annual 
electricity trade reaching 141 billion units, underscoring a 
17% growth over the previous year. This growth is especially 
significant given that the first half was shaped by softer demand 
conditions, demonstrating the underlying structural strength of 
exchange-based power trading.
The Real-Time Market (RTM) emerged as the defining growth 
story of FY’26. RTM volumes grew 41% year-on-year to 55 
billion units, now accounting for nearly 40% of total electricity 
volumes on IEX. This growth underscores the growing 
importance of flexibility in power procurement. As renewable 
energy becomes a larger share of India’s generation mix, the 
ability to respond in real-time to supply and demand variations 
becomes indispensable. 
The Green Market continued its steady progress, with traded 
volumes rising 23% over the previous year to 10.8 billion 
units. Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) trading remained 
active, with 187 lakh RECs traded, a 5% year-on-year increase,

segments to enable trading during high-demand morning and

growing at 7–8% per annum, the coming decade will demand 
significant investment in generation, transmission, storage, and 
market infrastructure. Power exchanges will be at the center

growth opportunities will shape our journey:

INDIAN ECONOMIC REVIEW
The Indian economy maintained its strong growth momentum 
for the most part in FY’26 despite the global economy passing 
through a phase of significant transition and uncertainty. In this 
global environment, India continued to stand out as one of the 
fastest-growing major economies in the world growing steadily 
by 7.7% in FY’26. India’s impressive growth has been supported 
by robust private consumption, sustained government capital 
expenditure, a resilient financial sector, and the continued 
beneficial effect of income-tax and GST rationalisation 
introduced in the Union Budget 2025-26.
The country is steadily moving towards becoming a global 
economic powerhouse and continues to be on track to become 
a 5 trillion-dollar economy by FY’30. While global economic 
uncertainty is expected to remain elevated in FY’27 the RBI 
expects India’s GDP growth to average 6.6 per cent based on 
heightened risks of inflationary pressures, supply disruptions 
and slower global growth. On the domestic front, the Indian 
Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast a below-
normal South-West monsoon for 2026 at approximately 92% 
of the Long-Period Average (LPA), partly influenced by the 
development of El Niño conditions. This presents a headwind 
for the agricultural sector and rural consumption for FY’27.

INDIA’S POWER SECTOR
Countrywide electricity demand in FY’26 was 1,707 BUs, a 
marginal year-on-year increase of approximately 1%, reflecting 
a moderation in the pace of demand growth over FY’25. 
The slowdown was primarily driven by an early onset of the 
Southwest monsoon in May 2025, which reduced cooling needs 
and agricultural pump usage, compressing cooling-degree 
days significantly. Nevertheless, India’s long-run power demand 
drivers of rising income levels, rapid urbanisation, government 
electrification initiatives, expanding manufacturing, and electric 
vehicle adoption remain firmly intact. 
The power sector continued its rapid structural transformation 
in FY’26 with record-breaking capacity addition. India’s total 
installed generation capacity reached 533 GW as on 31st 
March 2026, an addition of 58 GW in a single year, the highest-
ever annual increment. India’s renewable installed capacity 
(excluding large hydro) crossed 230 GW, driven by record 
solar additions. A total of 55 GW of non-fossil capacity was 
added, the highest ever in a single year. Solar capacity surged 
to approximately 150 GW, while wind capacity rose to 57 GW. 
Total non-fossil capacity as on 31st March 2026 stood at 283 
GW (including large hydro and nuclear).Renewables (including 
large hydro) now account for approximately 53% of total 
installed capacity, a milestone. During this fiscal, India achieved 
50% non-fossil installed capacity nearly five years ahead of its 
2030 target.

This fiscal also witnessed growing grid integration challenges

Both the Government and the private sector are actively

Project, and the National Green Hydrogen Mission. All these

emissions intensity of its GDP by 45% by 2030 (relative to

India aims to establish a Green Hydrogen production capacity 
of at least 5 million metric tonnes annually by 2030 and the

Energy Mission, announced in FY’26, adds nuclear power as a 
key pillar of India’s long-term energy security strategy, targeting

SHANTI Act, 2025. The PM Surya Ghar Yojana continued to

DISTRIBUTION
In FY’23, the Ministry of Power introduced the Electricity (Late 
Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules to bolster 
the financial viability of the power sector. These rules were 
subsequently amended in FY’24 to address un-requisitioned 
surplus power. In FY’25, the National Load Dispatch Centre 
(NLDC) revised the procedure to include State-owned 
generating stations, with mock runs for penalties on generators 
commencing from July 2025. In FY’26, these rules became 
fully operational, further enhancing generator compliance, 
improving payment discipline and power market liquidity. 
Over the past few years, the government has introduced key 
measures to strengthen power distribution:
•	
Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS): The 
implementation of RDSS has continued to incentivise 
utilities under the `3 lakh crore scheme, targeting reduction 
of pan-India AT&C losses to 12–15% and the ACS-ARR 
gap to zero. The progress has been steady, with smart 
meter deployment reaching 22% of approved installations 
as of December 2025. Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs were 
mandated for all non-agricultural users from April 2025, 
aligning consumption patterns with solar generation.
•	
Additional Borrowing Scheme: State Governments 
continue to access additional borrowings of up to 0.5% 
of GSDP, conditioned on undertaking and sustaining 
power sector reforms to ensure financial viability of their 
Discoms.
•	
Prudential Lending Norms: Additional norms targeting 
financially stressed utilities remain in force. Discoms 
failing to meet defined improvement trajectories remain 
ineligible for borrowings from PFC and REC.
•	
Automatic Fuel Cost Pass Through: Several States have 
continued to employ automatic fuel and power purchase 
cost 
adjustment 
mechanisms, 
ensuring 
financial 
sustainability of Discoms.
•	
Integrated Discom Ratings: Earlier in March, the 14th 
Annual Integrated Rating and Ranking Report for 65 
Discoms was released, evaluating their financial health, 
performance excellence and responsiveness to external 
factors. According to the report, 41 utilities were able to 
achieve reduction in AT&C losses. A total of 22 utilities 
recorded an improvement in their ratings, while 30 utilities 
maintained their existing ratings. AT&C losses reduced for 
39 utilities in FY’25, with 38 utilities achieving AT&C losses 
below 15%, reflecting enhanced operational efficiency.

have declined from nearly 16.0% in FY’24 to 15.0% in

ECONOMIC EXPANSION AND POWER MARKETS
Industrial Growth and Urbanisation
Industrial growth and urbanisation remain key elements in 
India’s economic development and ongoing power sector 
transformation. The Government’s thrust on Atmanirbhar Bharat 
and policy measures to position India as the cornerstone of 
the China Plus One strategy for global businesses augmented 
exports and domestic productive capacities in FY’26. This was 
despite global trade uncertainties. These policy measures 
continue to drive increased electricity demand from the 
manufacturing sectors.
India has achieved notable strides in urbanisation. It is 
projected that by 2030, over 40% of India’s population will be 
living in cities. Although these cities occupy only about 3% 
of the country’s total land area, they remarkably generate 
60% of India’s GDP. India’s rapid urbanisation is projected to 
significantly increase energy consumption. Further, expected 
electricity demand from the growth of AI and data centres is 
also factored into the planning process of the government as it 
reinforces long-term demand projections. This AI growth boom 
is driven by cloud adoption, data localization mandates, and 
localized Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) workloads. As per 
the Ministry of Power, electricity demand from data centres is 
estimated to touch nearly 14 GW by FY’32. The strong growth 
in data centre demand is likely to trigger parallel demand for up 
to 50 GW of renewable energy. In the near term power demand 
is expected to touch almost 2,700 BUs with a peak demand of 
388 GW by FY’32.
Demand and Supply
According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), all India 
energy consumption reached approximately 1,707 Billion Units 
(BU) in FY’26, representing a year-on-year growth of about 1.1% 
from 1,692 BU in FY’25. The moderation in demand growth 
was primarily driven by an early onset of the monsoon in May 
2025, which reduced cooling degree days by more than 7% 
compared to 2024, with a 12% decline in June alone, a month 
which typically accounts for about 15% of annual demand. The 
peak demand met during the summer in FY’26 was 242 GW 
recorded in June 2025, while in June FY’25 peak demand stood 
at 245 GW.
The Northern Region remained the largest contributor to 
demand, though due to weather related events growth rates 
varied significantly across regions in FY’26. Key States such 
as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Uttar 
Pradesh recorded the highest peak demand levels.

reliance on dynamic and competitive electricity procurement 
methods to meet rising energy demands and enhance market 
efficiency.
OUTLOOK
In FY’26, India demonstrated remarkable resilience in navigating 
a complex global environment characterised by geopolitical 
tensions, evolving trade policies, and climate-linked demand 
volatility. India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals, robust 
private consumption, fiscal consolidation, and sustained public 
capex continue to underpin healthy power demand growth over 
the medium term. With India firmly on its trajectory to remain 
the world’s fastest-growing major economy, the power market 
is well-positioned to capitalise on annual incremental demand 
of nearly 100 BUs projected through 2030. The accelerating 
shift towards renewables, rising need for market-based storage 
dispatch supported by the government’s push on addition of 
BESS and PSP, introduction of newer market mechanisms, 
the structural load shifts in agriculture, and expansion of open 
access participation provide sustained growth levers for power 
market development.

during solar hours.

resulted in sell-side liquidity which was higher by nearly

CORE BUSINESS GROWTH
Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) has been actively working to 
deepen and diversify the short-term power market while

has continuously enhanced market flexibility by introducing 
innovative products and extending contract tenures to better 
meet the evolving requirements of market participants. To 
further strengthen the market and provide participants with 
greater flexibility in procurement and portfolio management, 
IEX has filed petitions with the Hon’ble CERC seeking approvals 
on new segments that would deepen power markets and 
strengthen the foundation for sustainable growth and 
innovation. Through continuous market development, product 
innovation, and the introduction of new market mechanisms. 
IEX aims to create a more robust, efficient, and future-ready 
electricity market ecosystem. The following areas serve as the 
cornerstone of our vision and drive our core business growth:
•	 Power Procurement Optimisation by Discoms
	 With over 90 distribution companies currently registered, 
IEX works closely with these utilities to reduce their power 
procurement expenses by leveraging cost-competitive 
merit order scheduling. The exchange assists utilities in 
both short-term bilateral contracts and long-term Power 
Purchase Agreements (PPAs) by identifying opportunities to 
replace expensive power with more affordable alternatives 
available on its platform. This strategy enables distribution 
companies to realize substantial cost savings. Furthermore, 
IEX actively supports these utilities through ongoing 
capacity-building and educational programs, ensuring they 
are well-equipped to maximize the value and efficiency of 
their power procurement activities.
•	 Growing Open Access Procurement  
	 Electricity remains one of the most significant cost 
components for industries. In energy-intensive sectors such 
as cement, metals, automobiles, chemicals and paper, power 
procurement can account for nearly 50% of operating costs. 
Power exchanges provide open-access consumers with the 
flexibility to supplement their power requirements based on 
prevailing market conditions. Transparent price discovery and 
a range of short-duration products allow consumers to align 
procurement decisions with production schedules, demand 
patterns and generation availability. Over 5,900 commercial 
and industrial consumers across India utilise IEX’s platform 
to procure competitively priced power. These prices provided 
an opportunity for open-access consumers to optimize their 
power procurement costs throughout the year in FY’26, 
rather than being solely dependent on discom procurement. 
It also provided an opportunity to replace costlier power from 
captive generation with more competitively priced power 
available through the exchange. Reflecting this growing 
value proposition, participation by open-access consumers 
on power exchanges has increased significantly, with traded 
volumes growing by over 50% year-on-year Several States 
are also encouraging renewable energy procurement through 
Green Markets on power exchanges supported policies that 
provide exemptions from additional surcharge. The Ministry 
of Power over the last few years has introduced significant 
amendments to Electricity Rules, enabling large industrial 
users to establish their own transmission lines and grid 
connections without requiring a license. To further promote 
open access, IEX actively engages with potential consumers, 
raises awareness and advocates for policy and regulatory 
reforms at both the Central and State levels. Our efforts 
aim to address systemic challenges and remove tariff and 
non-tariff barriers, ensuring seamless access to competitive 
power procurement.

part of our strategy to deepen and diversify the short-term 
power market, IEX has filed petitions with the Hon’ble CERC

and the extension of Term-Ahead Market (TAM) contracts

NEW OPPORTUNITIES
Battery Energy Storage Systems
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) remain a cornerstone 
of India’s clean energy transition, enabling seamless integration 
of renewable power into the national grid. In FY’24, the 
Ministry of Power introduced the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) 
mechanism to catalyse 4,000 MWh of BESS capacity, which 
was later expanded to 13,200 GWh in response to falling costs. 
Building on the success of Tranche I, the Ministry of Power 
launched VGF Tranche II with a target of 30,000 MWh, marking 
a significant scale up. By March FY’26, tenders totalling 43,000 
MWh had been floated, with nearly 40,000 MWh successfully 
awarded and the rest were in the tendering process stage. The 
pace of tender clearances has emerged as a clear reflection 
of strong policy execution and growing market confidence. 
BESS plays a dual role in the evolving energy landscape by 
storing surplus solar generation during solar hours (day-time) 
and dispatching electricity during evening peaks, while also 
stabilizing the grid during periods of high renewable penetration. 
One of the key operational models under consideration is the 
charge and discharge through power exchanges, where current 
prices range between `2.0–`2.5 per unit during solar hours and 
`5–`7 per unit in the evening, offering a compelling arbitrage 
opportunity for BESS operators. For an ISTS connected BESS 
project for 2-hrs BESS including ISTS losses and Round-trip 
efficiency (RtE), the annual arbitrage is around `4.81/unit 
(with 545 annual cycles) and for a 4-hrs BESS project the 
annual arbitrage is around `3.91/unit (with 484 annual cycles). 
With falling discovered tariffs, expectations of further cost 
reductions, and expanding participation in ancillary services, 
BESS has firmly established itself as a commercially viable and 
strategically essential component of India’s energy ecosystem.
Market-based Models
Deepening India’s green power markets is essential to reduce 
cost of renewable energy integration and generating efficient 
price signals that can guide new capacity addition. IEX continues 
to advocate for greater market-based participation in green 
power trading, including recommending 10–15% of power 
from all new RE projects awarded by REIAs and DISCOMs to 
be mandatorily channelled through the green market segments 
of power exchanges, a measure that would materially enhance 
liquidity and price transparency.
In a significant structural development in FY’26, CERC approved 
IEX’s proposal to revamp its Green Contracts framework, 
replacing the earlier Solar, Non-Solar, and Hydro classifications 
with four new categories — Wind, Hydro, Distributed Renewable 
Energy (DRE), and Other RE which are in alignment with 
the Ministry of Power’s revised Renewable Consumption 
Obligation (RCO) notification of September 2025. The revised 
framework applies across IEX’s full suite of green market 
products, including the Green Day Ahead Market (G-DAM), 
Green Day Ahead Contingency (G-DAC), Green Intra-Day 
Contracts, and Green Daily, Weekly, and Monthly Contracts, in 
effect, strengthening the alignment between exchange-traded 
green power and India’s evolving clean energy compliance 
architecture.
With regards Virtual Power Purchase Agreement (VPPA), FY’26 
marked a landmark regulatory milestone. CERC finalised the 
VPPA Guidelines through a notification dated December 24, 
2025, published in the Gazette on January 28, 2026, providing 
a structured and legally certain pathway for designated 
consumers and corporates to procure renewable energy 
attributes without the need for physical power delivery. Under 
this framework, the renewable energy generator sells power 
independently on exchanges such as IEX, while the difference 
between the market-discovered price and the pre-agreed 
reference price is settled bilaterally  with Renewable Energy 
Certificates (RECs) transferred to the consumer to enable 
Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO) compliance.
These guidelines mark a significant milestone in India’s journey 
towards energy transition, providing a credible and structured 
instrument for corporates to meet their green procurement 
goals.  The VPPA model is posed to gain significant traction 
among Commercial & Industrial (C&I) consumers as corporates 
accelerate their decarbonisation commitments while retaining 
operational flexibility in power scheduling. Beyond compliance, 
VPPAs are increasingly being recognised as an effective long-
term price hedging instrument for C&I customers, offering 
revenue certainty to RE developers while insulating buyers from 
market price volatility. 
As a fillip to the Contract for Difference (CfD) model, the Ministry 
of New and Renewable Energy of India (MNRE) has approved a 
500 MW pilot CfD for RE on a 3-hour basis to be implemented by 
Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI). This pilot shall enable 
RE generators to sell electricity on power exchanges, while 
SECI settles the difference between the discovered strike price 
and the reference market price. The pilot would supply 1,500

The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana - the world’s largest 
domestic rooftop solar initiative has provided significant 
impetus to the growth of distributed energy resources and 
the emergence of local energy markets, including Peer-to-
Peer (P2P) electricity trading. As of March 2026, the scheme 
has benefited over 32 lakh households through rooftop solar 
installations and lifted cumulative RTS capacity to 25.7 GW, a 
51% increase on a year on year basis, with more than 63 lakh 
applications received on the scheme portal and disbursal 
of `14,771 crore through Central Financial Assistance. With 
rooftop solar capacity scaling rapidly, the energy ecosystem is 
at an inflection point, necessitating a gradual transition from 
subsidy-driven mechanisms such as Net Metering towards a 
more dynamic, market-based framework such as P2P trading 
that better reflect the true value of distributed generation.
P2P electricity trading has been gaining traction globally, driven 
by the proliferation of prosumers-households and entities 
that both generate and consume energy. India is witnessing 
encouraging momentum on this front. In February 2026, REC 
Limited, the nodal agency for the India Energy Stack under the 
Ministry of Power showcased the first-ever live demonstration 
of a peer-to-peer decentralised energy transaction under 
the India Energy Stack (IES) framework, underscoring the 
Government’s commitment to enabling technology-driven 
local energy markets. Under the India Energy Stack, consumers 
generating renewable energy through rooftop solar systems will 
be able to trade surplus electricity with other users, including 
across State borders, operating on a secure, trust-based digital 
framework to ensure transactions are verifiable and scalable.
The P2P initiative is currently being positioned as a policy 
sandbox, with its immediate objective being digital validation 
in terms of testing identity management, smart meter data 
exchange, interoperable APIs, price discovery tools, billing 
integration, and settlement systems within a controlled 
environment. The pilot focuses primarily on rooftop solar 
prosumers which includes residential, commercial, and 
institutional consumers equipped with smart meters at 
distribution voltage levels.
States such as Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, and Delhi have taken 
the lead in issuing guidelines and regulations to govern and 
promote P2P trading, while others such as Assam and Odisha 
are advancing regulatory frameworks to support decentralized 
energy markets. As rooftop solar capacities continue to 
scale under the PM Surya Ghar scheme, it is expected that 
more States will progressively establish enabling regulatory 
frameworks, paving the way for a vibrant, decentralised energy 
market ecosystem in India.
Carbon Market
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) has undergone 
significant evolution, emerging as the mainstay of India’s 
market-based climate action framework. Following its 2023 
amendment to include the Offset Mechanism, the scheme 
now encompasses both obligated entities with binding targets 
and non-obligated entities that may voluntarily participate 
by purchasing Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) to fulfil their 
sustainability commitments.
The CCTS operates as an intensity-based baseline-and-credit 
system, with targets defined as tonnes of CO2₂ equivalent 
per unit of product output. Entities that outperform their 
assigned targets will be eligible to earn CCCs, which can be 
traded on power exchanges. Conversely, entities falling short 
of their targets will be required to purchase and surrender 
equivalent CCCs to achieve compliance. The scheme is jointly 
administered by the Ministry of Power, MoEFCC, and the 
Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), with the Central Electricity 
Regulatory Commission (CERC) providing regulatory oversight. 
In January 2026, emission‑intensity targets were notified 
for seven energy‑intensive sectors - Aluminium, Cement, 
Chlor‑Alkali, Pulp & Paper, Petroleum Refining, Petrochemicals, 
and Textiles -covering approximately 490 entities with legally 
binding obligations for FY’26 and FY’27, using FY’24 as the 
baseline year. The baseline emission‑intensity target for FY’24 
was 480.25 tCO2e per tonne of equivalent product, while the 
cumulative emission target for FY’26 was reduced to 476.57 
tCO2e per tonne, reflecting India’s progressive decarbonization 
trajectory. 
Offsets are generated through accredited renewable energy, 
energy efficiency, and afforestation projects, validated under 
the supervision of the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) and 
aligned with Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement. Under the offset 
mechanism BEE has approved 10 sectors and 12 methodologies 
for buying and selling CCCs on power exchanges which will 
increase the trading of such CCCs.
With the first compliance period now underway, obligated 
entities were required to submit their action plans to BEE by 
April 2026, followed by verified MRV reporting for FY’26 by July 
2026. CCC trading on the designated exchange is expected to 
formally open by October 2026, marking the beginning of active 
price discovery in India’s carbon market.

for Coal Exchanges.

MARKET COUPLING
CERC vide its order dated 06 February 2024, directed Grid India 
to carry out pilot study to assess the impact of market coupling. 
As per the Grid India report, increase in economic surplus was 
0.3% which is insignificant. Based on the submissions made 
by Grid-India, CERC, vide its order dated 23 July 2025, decided 
to initiate the process for implementing market coupling of the 
Day-Ahead Market (DAM) and directed staff of commission 
to frame procedure and regulation for the implementation of 
same.
As per the order, with respect to the Real-Time Market (RTM), 
given the shorter time for bid submission and running the 
market clearing engine, the decision to implement the coupling 
of Real-Time Market (RTM) of the power exchanges shall be 
considered at a later stage after gaining operational experience 
from the coupling of DAM. Additionally, the feasibility of coupling 
the Term-Ahead Market (including Contingency Contracts) of 
the power exchanges shall be examined through a shadow 
pilot.
The CERC Order of July 2025 was challenged before the Appellate 
Tribunal of Electricity (APTEL) by IEX on various points of its 
legality, transparency and on merits. In February 2026, APTEL 
dismissed the Appeal citing IEX is not a “person aggrieved” at 
this stage since market coupling to be implemented through 
regulations to be notified separately by CERC and the CERC 
Order of July 2025 is merely “administrative” and “tentative”. 
APTEL further preserved IEX rights to appeal on merits after 
framing of the regulations by CERC. 
Subsequently, IEX filed a Civil Appeal with stay application in 
Supreme Court against the APTEL judgement on 10th April 
2026. 
On 17th April 2026, CERC issued a draft amendment to PMR 
2021 for implementation of market coupling with Grid-India as 
the MCO. Public hearings on the draft regulations concluded on 
10th June 2026.

payment, security management and collateral management.

of a cyberattack but also the potential consequences, such as 
financial loss, reputational damage, or operational disruption.

Building on the success of API-based bidding, IEX introduced 
the Backoffice API, providing seamless access to post-trade 
reports such as delivery schedules and financial obligation 
reports.  Nearly 72% of the cleared volume in I-DAM are 
contributed by members using APIs. The Company remains 
focused on expanding API functionalities to enable greater 
automation, faster response to market dynamics and deeper 
integration with customers’ systems.
Leveraging nearly two decades of customer relationships, the 
Business Development team continues to work closely with 
market participants through workshops and advisory support, 
enabling them to optimise power procurement strategies and 
maximise value from exchange-based trading. Integration of 
front-end trading, back-office reporting and customer SAP 
systems, together with data analytics-led bidding tools and 
a unified margining framework, further enhances operational 
efficiency and the overall trading experience.
With increasing electrification, improving supply liquidity, 
new market models, supportive policy initiatives and ongoing 
diversification efforts, IEX remains well positioned to 
capitalise on the significant growth opportunities in the Indian 
power market and deliver sustainable long-term value for 
stakeholders. We believe that the impact of market coupling 
would be minimal. 
STRATEGIC RISK
The government, in its various vision documents, has 
emphasised the need for a deeper and transparent power 
market in India. Being a regulated organisation with rules, bye 
laws, business rules and circulars approved by the Central 
Electricity Regulatory Commission, IEX functions within the 
ambit of provisions and remains on top of all the compliances. 
The Company is also regulated by various regulations under 
the Electricity Act 2003 such as Power Market Regulations, 
Inter-State Open Access (OA) Regulations and Procedure for 
Scheduling of Collective Transactions issued by POSOCO, 
etc. Any deviation from any of the provisions under these 
regulations would be of significant risk to IEX.
Mitigation: The Enterprise Risk Management Committee 
meetings are held on a half yearly basis, where regulatory, 
strategic, operational and technology & cybersecurity risks 
are presented along with mitigation measures. Also, from 
the regulatory perspective, both the Market Surveillance 
Committee and the Risk Assessment and Management 
Committee are constituted as mandated by the Central 
Electricity Regulatory Commission. The committee meetings 
are held as per timelines fixed by the Central Electricity 
Regulatory Commission with reports submitted to the regulator 
at regular intervals. The State level regulations are governed by 
State Electricity Regulatory Commissions. The Company also 
proactively engages in regular policy advocacy with the Central 
Electricity Regulatory Commission, State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions, Ministry of Power and other industry bodies for 
any change in regulation that may adversely affect its business.
OPERATIONAL RISK
Operational risks have the potential to affect the regular 
business operations of the Company. This may include 
factors such as margin maintenance, access to trading data, 
sufficient bank balance in settlement account for meeting the 
requirement of executing trades, etc.
Mitigation: Mitigation measures include regular surveillance of 
the trading mechanism and reporting any error to the Central 
Electricity Regulatory Commission at periodic intervals.
Moreover, the Company is ISO 9001:2015 certified with 
definitive Standard Operating Procedures in place.
TECHNOLOGY RISK
The introduction of various new products with stringent 
timelines has increased dependency on the use of latest

Platform Robustness and Reliability: Our technology platform 
is designed to deliver solutions, meeting highest standards 
of performance and security that empower our clients for 
seamless energy trading. IEX has built a robust and advanced 
IT ecosystem and is designed to handle high volumes of 
transactions with high availability, scalability and security for 
the Exchange to operate 24x7x365. We continuously invest 
effort and resources in technology to elevate its ease, 24*7 
availability, reliability, security and to provide the best-in-class 
experience to our customers. We have always endeavored to 
advance technology architecture at the Exchange Platform 
level as well as at the Enterprise level. Over the years, we have 
successfully transitioned from monolithic software to more 
modular service-based architecture. With key functionalities 
such as anonymous order matching, real-time reference 
pricing, and dynamic margin monitoring, the platform ensures 
price transparency and delivers prompt, reliable order routing, 
trade reporting, and market data dissemination, all while 
maintaining robust market surveillance. Central to this trading 
system is the highly trusted matching engine, which has 
consistently earned the confidence of market participants. This 
engine not only facilitates efficient and rapid price discovery 
but is also engineered to maximize Social Welfare in line with 
CERC Power Market Regulations. Our trading platform provides 
members with the flexibility to place bids using Web interface 
and Application Programming Interface (API). 
Application security is a critical aspect in IEX which aims 
at protecting applications from security threats throughout 
their lifecycle. Considering the challenges of evolving threat 
landscape, complexity of modern applications, IEX has adapted 
AAA (Authentication, Authorization and Accounting) solutions 
and MFA (Multi Factor Authentication) which ensures that only 
legitimate users and processes can access an application 
and its resources. Encryption (AES-256 CBC) in Bid Data, 
secure data storage, encrypted communication channels 
(TLS1.2 and above) and data masking technologies ensures 
safeguarding sensitive data from unauthorized access and 
ensuring compliance with regulations. Strong token-based 
authentication mechanism, rate limiting, and input validation 
etc. are implemented to maintain security and reliability in APIs. 
Implementation of appropriate application hardening measures 
are also in practice which includes removing unnecessary 
features, applying patches, configuring security settings, 
implementing anti-debugging techniques, input validation, 
proper error handling etc.  In IEX, applications are scanned on 
regular frequency and prior to rolling out any major upgrades 
in Production to identify and address the latest Vulnerabilities 
if any. This involves secure code review, VA scan through tools 
and penetration testing as well.

responsibility for ensuring that the Company has implemented

with reference to:

Effectiveness and efficiency of operations
•	
Reliability of financial reporting

At IEX, Internal Financial Controls forms an integral part of the 
Company’s risk management process which in turn is a part 
of Corporate Governance addressing financial and financial 
reporting risks. The Company has a well-established Internal 
Control Framework including proper delegation of authority, 
policies, and procedures, defined various internal controls, risk 
based internal audits, risk management framework and whistle 
blower mechanism, which is designed to continuously assess 
the adequacy, effectiveness, and efficiency of financial and 
operational controls. The management is committed to ensuring 
an effective internal control environment, commensurate with 
the size and complexity of the business, which provides an 
assurance on compliance with internal policies, applicable 
laws, regulations and protection of resources and assets.

of conduct, conflict of interest, confidentiality, and whistle 
blower policy) and other polices (like organization structure, HR 
policy, IT security policy and business continuity and disaster 
recovery plan). The Company has also defined Standard 
Operating Procedures (SOP) for each of its processes to guide 
the operations in an ethical and compliant manner.

accordingly, the Directors’ Responsibility Statement contains 
confirmation as regards the adequacy of the IFC. Assurances 
on the effectiveness of IFC is obtained through management 
reviews, self-assessment, continuous monitoring by functional 
heads as well as testing of the internal financial control systems 
by the internal and external auditors during the course of their 
audit. The Internal control system is improved and modified on 
an on-going basis to meet the changes in business conditions, 
accounting, and statutory requirements.

efficiency of these systems and procedures on regular basis to 
ensure that all the assets of the Company are protected against 
any loss and that the financial and operational information 
is accurate and complete in all respects. The Audits are 
conducted on an ongoing basis and significant deviations, if 
any, are brought to the notice of the Audit Committee following 
which corrective action is recommended for implementation.

/irregularities and early remedial steps.

RISK MANAGEMENT 
Risk Management is a critical element in the operation of an 
exchange business and constitutes an integral part of the 
Company’s corporate governance framework. The Company 
believes that a robust risk management framework enables 
the establishment of effective control systems and monitoring 
mechanisms, thereby ensuring the smooth, efficient, and 
resilient functioning of its operations. Being a power exchange, 
the Company has put in place adequate risk management 
systems and procedures that are commensurate with the 
nature, size, and complexity of its business.
The Company has adopted a comprehensive Risk Management 
Policy approved by the Board, which provides a structured 
and enterprise-wide approach for identification, assessment, 
monitoring, and mitigation of risks. The framework covers a 
wide spectrum of risks, including market, credit, operational, 
regulatory, technological, and cyber risks, which may impact 
the business and its strategic objectives. The risk management 
process is aligned with applicable regulatory requirements and 
leading risk management practices, and is regularly reviewed 
to ensure its continued relevance in a dynamic business 
environment. The said Policy was reviewed and amended by 
the Board during the year to ensure its continued alignment 
with the evolving business requirements and changing global 
landscape.
The key cornerstones of the Company’s Risk Management 
Framework are as follows:
•	
A comprehensive Risk Management Policy providing an 
enterprise-wide framework;
•	
Periodic identification, assessment, and prioritization of 
risks impacting the Company’s business and objectives;
•	
Development and implementation of appropriate risk 
mitigation strategies to manage and reduce exposure to 
identified risks;
•	
Continued focus on effective execution and monitoring of 
mitigation measures;
•	
A 
structured 
review 
and 
monitoring 
mechanism 
involving functional teams, senior management, the Risk 
Management Committees, the Audit Committee, and the 
Board for oversight of key risks and mitigation plans;
•	
Integration of risk management considerations into 
strategic planning, annual operating plans, and key business 
decisions;
•	
Continuous monitoring of the external environment to 
identify emerging risks and evolving risk trends; and
•	
Strengthening of internal controls and adoption of risk 
appetite principles, wherever applicable, to ensure that risks 
are managed within acceptable limits.

Enterprise Risk Management Committee (ERMC), and Risk 
Assessment and Management Committee (RAMC). This

PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF THE BOARD
The Board of Directors has carried out an annual evaluation of its own performance, Board Committees, and Individual Directors 
pursuant to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Corporate Governance requirements as prescribed by the SEBI 
Listing Regulations. 
The annual evaluation process involved assessment of Individual Directors, Chairman and Managing Director of the Board, and 
the Chairman of the respective Board Committees. Further, the Independent Directors evaluated the performance of all the Non-
Independent Directors, Chairman and Managing Director of the Board, Board Committees, and the Board as a whole. Thereafter, 
the Board evaluated the performance of each Independent Director, excluding the Director being evaluated.
The criteria for performance evaluation, inter alia, include the following:
i.	
Individual Director’s Performance Evaluation
	
Compliance with Articles of Association, Companies Act & other laws, attendance at meetings, being informed and the extent 
of preparedness for meetings, participation and contribution, independence of judgment, leadership initiative and advisory 
role, interpersonal relationships with other directors and management, knowledge updation, displaying initiative, expressing 
views, understanding of the Company and the external environment, safeguarding stakeholders’ interest and balancing the 
conflict of interest of stakeholders, confidentiality, financial and risk awareness.
ii.	
Evaluation of the Board as a Whole
	
Proper mix of competencies, experience and qualification, adoption of proper, clear and transparent procedure to appoint 
directors, conducting meeting(s) on a regular basis, confirming agenda with all relevant information, providing entrepreneurial 
leadership to the Company, understanding of business, strategy and growth, responsibility towards stakeholders, risk 
management and financial controls and audits, compliances, discussions through healthy debate, quality of decision 
making, monitoring performance of management, reviewing the CSR initiatives, grievance redressal mechanism, analyse 
and examines governance and compliances related issues, maintaining high standards of integrity and probity, etc.
iii.	
Chairman & Managing Director’s Performance Evaluation
	
Providing effective leadership, setting effective strategic agenda of the Board, encouraging active engagement by the Board 
members, establishing effective communication with all stakeholders, and successful execution of business plans, risk 
management, achievement of business targets, development of plans and policies aligned to the vision and mission of the 
company, etc.
iv.	
Performance Evaluation of Board Committees
	
Sufficiency in the scope for addressing the objectives, effectiveness in performing the key responsibilities, adequacy in 
composition and frequency of meetings, quality of relationship of the committee with the board and the management, clarity 
of agenda discussed, discussion on critical issues, clarity of role and responsibilities, etc.

POLICY TO PROMOTE DIVERSITY ON THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS 
1.	
PREFACE
	
Indian Energy Exchange Limited (the “Company”) is committed to deal with all stakeholders with full transparency and 
fairness, ensuring adherence to all laws and regulations and achieving highest standards of corporate governance.
	
Pursuant to Regulation 19(4) read with Part D of the Schedule II of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, the nomination and 
remuneration committee of the board of directors of a listed entity is required to devise a policy on diversity of board of 
directors In compliance with the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, the Company has formulated the policy on diversity of board of 
directors
2.	
DEFINITIONS
	
For the purpose of this Board Diversity Policy the following terms shall have the meanings assigned to them hereunder:
(i)	
“Board” means the board of directors of the Company;
(ii)	
“Board Diversity Policy” means this policy, as amended from time to time;
(iii)	 “CERC Power Market Regulations” means the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Power Market) Regulations, 
2010;
(iv)	 “Committee” means the Nomination and Remuneration Committee of the Board;
(v)	
“Director” means a member of the Board;
(vi)	 “IEX” or the “Company” means Indian Energy Exchange Limited; and
(vii)	 “SEBI (LODR) Regulations” means the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015.
	
Words and expressions used and not defined in this Board Diversity Policy shall have the meaning ascribed to them in the 
SEBI (LODR) Regulations, the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 
1956, the Depositories Act, 1996 or the Companies Act, 2013 and rules and regulations made thereunder.
3.	
BOARD DIVERSITY
•	
The Committee shall ensure that the Board shall have an optimum combination of executive, non-executive and 
independent directors in accordance with requirements of the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI (LODR) Regulations, CERC 
Power Market Regulations and other statutory, regulatory and contractual obligations of the Company. 
•	
The Company recognises the benefits of having a diverse Board and sees increasing diversity at Board level as an 
essential element in maintaining a competitive advantage. The Company believes that a truly diverse Board will leverage 
differences in thought, perspective, knowledge, skill, regional and industry experience, cultural and geographical 
background, age, race and gender, which will ensure that the Company retains its competitive advantage. The Company 
further believes that a diverse Board will contribute towards driving business results, make corporate governance more 
effective, enhance quality and responsible decision-making capability, ensure sustainable development and enhance 
the reputation of the Company.
•	
The Committee shall review the profile of the prospective candidates for appointment as director on the Board taking in 
consideration knowledge, experience, financial literacy / expertise, global market awareness and other relevant factors 
as may be considered appropriate and the Board shall be so formulated with mix of members to maintain high level of 
ethical standards. The Committee shall also take into consideration the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, SEBI 
(LODR) Regulations and other statutory, regulatory and contractual obligations of the Company.
4.	
AMENDMENTS TO THE POLICY
	
The Committee may modify and/or amend the Board Diversity Policy at any time subject to the provisions of the SEBI (LODR) 
Regulations and the Companies Act, 2013 and rules framed thereunder.

This section is aimed at helping businesses demonstrate the structures, policies and processes put in place towards adopting the

referred as P1-P9 as given below:   
P1
Businesses should conduct and govern themselves with integrity in a manner that is ethical, transparent, and accountable.
P2
Businesses should provide goods and services in a manner that is sustainable and safe.
P3
Businesses should respect and promote the well-being of all employees, including those in their value chains. 
P4
Businesses should respect the interests of and be responsive towards all its stakeholders.
P5

IEX remains steadfast in its vision to architect next-generation sustainable energy solutions through innovation such 
as the Green Market segment, the Real-Time Market, the Certificate segment, underpinned by ESG principles across its 
business. This vision also aligns with and is reinforced by the Government of India’s initiatives to promote a sustainable 
way of life through the development of the Indian Carbon Market.
The Company is ISO 14001:2015 certified for environmental management systems and continues to align its operations 
with India’s long-term sustainability goals. IEX maintained its carbon-neutral status throughout FY’23–FY’26, reflecting 
its sustained commitment to environmental stewardship and climate action. These efforts contribute towards India’s 
nationally determined contribution (NDC) target of reducing the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030, in line with 
global efforts to limit temperature rise to 1.5°C.
ICX, a wholly owned subsidiary of the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX), is the authorized local Issuer of International 
Renewable Energy Certificates (I-RECs) in India. Our commitment to sustainability and excellence along with our deep 
understanding of the Indian power sector ensures the highest standard in verifying and issuing I-RECs.
IEX ensures environmentally responsible disposal of e-waste generated from its IT assets through authorized 
government-certified e-waste recyclers. As a responsible stakeholder, IEX continues to invest in advanced technology 
infrastructure, strengthening its digital ecosystem with a strong focus on data protection and customer privacy. The 
Company remains committed to fostering inclusive and sustainable growth.
At IEX, we believe that sustainable business growth goes hand in hand with creating a positive impact on society. 
Guided by this belief, the Company continues to undertake meaningful Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives 
aimed at fostering sustainable and inclusive development. These initiatives are strategically focused on key areas 
such as environmental sustainability, socio-economic empowerment of underserved communities, promotion of 
social equity, education of the girl child, healthcare, preservation of culture and heritage, advancement of research, 
and disaster management, relief, and rehabilitation. Through these efforts, IEX supported more than 139 schools 
and institutions and positively impacted the lives of more than 3.5 lakh beneficiaries. These achievements reflect the 
Company’s enduring commitment to creating lasting social value, empowering communities, and contributing to a 
more inclusive and sustainable future for all. 
IEX recognizes that sustainability is integral to long-term business success. The integration of sustainability into 
reporting frameworks has enhanced transparency and strengthened the Company’s ability to demonstrate value

Supporting documents for revenue transactions related to electricity traded closer

applicable accounting standards.
