3.8 	 Employee Benefits
3.8.1 Short term employee benefits
 
All employee benefits payable wholly within twelve months of 
rendering the services are classified as short-term employee 
benefits. Benefits such as salaries, wages, bonus, etc. are 
recognized in the statement of profit and loss in the period in which 
the employee renders the related services.  Such obligations are 
measured on an undiscounted basis.
	
A liability is recognised for the amount expected to be paid 
under short-term cash bonus, if the Group has a present legal 
or constructive obligation to pay this amount as a result of past 
service provided by the employee and the obligation can be 
estimated reliably.
3.8.2 Defined contribution plan
 
A defined contribution plan is a post-employment benefit plan 
under which Group’s legal or constructive obligation is limited 
to the amount that it contributes to a separate legal entity. 
Obligations for contributions to defined contribution plans are 
recognized as an employee benefits expense in the statement of 
profit and loss in the period during which services are rendered by 
employees.
 
The Group pays fixed contribution to Provident Fund at 
predetermined rates to regional provident fund commissioner. 
The contributions to the fund for the year are recognized as 
expense and are charged to the statement of profit and loss in 
which the related services are provided by the employees.
3.8.3 Defined benefit plan
 
A defined benefit plan is a post-employment benefit plan other 
than a defined contribution plan. Group’s liability towards gratuity 
is in the nature of defined benefit plans.
 
Group’s net obligation in respect of defined benefit plan is 
calculated separately by estimating the amount of future benefit 
that employees have earned in return for their service in the 
current and prior periods; that benefit is discounted to determine 
its present value. Any unrecognized past service costs and the fair 
value of any plan assets are deducted. The discount rate is based 
on the prevailing market yields of Indian government securities as 
at the reporting date that have maturity dates approximating the 
terms of the Group’s obligations and that are denominated in the 
same currency in which the benefits are expected to be paid.
 
When the benefits of a plan are changed or when a plan is 
curtailed, the resulting change in benefit that relates to past 
service (‘past service cost’ or ‘past service gain’) or the gain or 
loss on curtailment is recognised immediately in Statement of 
profit and Loss. The Group recognises gains and losses on the 
settlement of a defined benefit plan when the settlement occurs.
 
The calculation is performed annually by a qualified actuary using 
the projected unit credit method. When the calculation results in 
a benefit to the Group, the recognized asset is limited to the total 
of any unrecognized past service costs. Any actuarial gains or 
losses are recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) in 
the period in which they arise.
3.8.4 Other long term employee benefits
 
Benefits under the Group’s compensated absences constitute 
other long term employee benefits.
 
Cost of long-term benefit by way of accumulating compensated 
absences arising during the tenure of the service is calculated 
taking into account the pattern of availment of leave. In respect of 
encashment of leave, the defined benefit is calculated taking into 
account all types of decrements and qualifying salary projected 
up to the assumed date of encashment. The present value of 
obligations under such long-term benefit plan is determined 
based on actuarial valuation carried out by an independent 
actuary using the Projected Unit Credit Method as at period end.
3.8.5 Share based payments
 
The grant date fair value of equity settled share-based payment 
awards granted to employees is recognized as an employee 
benefits expense, with a corresponding increase in other equity, 
over the vesting period of the award. The amount recognized as 
expense is adjusted to reflect the number of awards for which 
the related service and non-market performance conditions are 
expected to be met, such that the amount ultimately recognized 
as an expense is based on the number of awards that do meet 
the related service and non-market vesting conditions at the 
vesting date. For share-based payment awards with non-vesting 
conditions, the grant date fair value of the share-based payment 
is measured to reflect such conditions and there is no true-up for 
differences between expected and actual outcome.
 
When the terms of an equity-settled award are modified, the 
minimum expense recognised by the Group is the grant date of 
the unmodified award provided the vesting conditions (other than 
a market condition) specified on grant date of the award are met
	
Further, additional expense, if any, is measured and recognised as 
at the date of modification, in case such modification increases 
the total fair value of the share-based payment plan, or is 
otherwise beneficial to the employee.
3.9 	 Impairment of non-financial assets
 
The Group ‘s non-financial assets, other than deferred tax assets, 
are reviewed at each reporting date to determine whether there is 
any indication of impairment. If any such indication exists, then 
the asset’s recoverable amount is estimated. 
	
For assets that are not yet available for use, the recoverable 
amount is estimated at each reporting date.
 
The recoverable amount of an asset or cash-generating unit is 
the higher of its fair value less costs to disposal and its value in 
use. In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows 
are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount 
rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value 
of money and the risks specific to the asset. For the purpose of 
impairment testing, assets that cannot be tested individually are 
grouped together into the smallest group of assets that generates 
cash inflows from continuing use that are largely independent of 
the cash inflows of other assets or groups of assets (the “cash-
generating unit”, or “CGU”).
 
An impairment loss is recognized if the carrying amount of an 
asset or its CGU exceeds its estimated recoverable amount. 
Impairment losses are recognized in the statement of profit 
and loss. Impairment losses recognized in respect of CGUs are 
reduced from the carrying amounts of the assets of the CGU.
 
Impairment losses recognized in prior periods are assessed 
at each reporting date for any indications that the loss has 
decreased or no longer exists. An impairment loss is reversed

3.10  Leases
3.10.1 Accounting for operating leases- As a lessee
	
The Group’s lease assets classes primarily consist of lease for 
office premises. The Group assesses whether a contract contains 
a lease, at inception of a contract. A contract is, or contains, a 
lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an 
identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. 
To assess whether a contract conveys the right to control the use 
of an identified asset, the Group assesses whether: 
a) 
the contract involves the use of an identified asset 
b) 
the Group has substantially all of the economic benefits 
from use of the asset through the period of the lease and 
the Group has the right to direct the use of the asset.
 
At the date of commencement of the lease, the Group recognizes 
a right-of-use asset (“ROU”) and a corresponding lease liability 
for all lease arrangements in which it is a lessee, except for leases 
with a term of twelve months or less (short-term leases) and 
low value leases. For these short-term and low value leases, the 
Group recognizes the lease payments as an operating expense 
on a straight-line basis over the term of the lease. Certain lease 
arrangements include the options to extend or terminate the 
lease before the end of the lease term. ROU assets and lease 
liabilities includes these options when it is reasonably certain 
that they will be exercised. The right-of-use assets are initially 
recognized at cost, which comprises the initial amount of the 
lease liability adjusted for any lease payments made at or prior to 
the commencement date of the lease plus any initial direct costs 
incurred and an estimate of costs to dismantle and remove the 
underlying asset or to restore the underlying asset or the site on 
which its is located, less any lease incentives received. They are 
subsequently measured at cost less accumulated depreciation 
and impairment losses.
 
Right-of-use assets is subsequently depreciated using the 
straight-line method from the commencement date to the earlier 
of the end of the useful life of the right-of-use asset or the end 
of the lease term, unless the lease transfers ownership of the 
underlying asset to the Group by the end of the lease term or the 
cost of the right-of-use-asset reflects that the Group will exercise 
a purchase option. In that case, the right-of-use asset will be 
depreciated over the useful life of the underlying asset, which is 
determined on the same basis as those of property, plant and 
equipment. In addition, the Right-of-use asset is periodically 
reduced by impairment losses, if any, and adjusted for certain 
remeasurements of the lease liability. 
	
The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the 
lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date, 
discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease or, if that rate 
cannot be readily determined, the Group’s incremental borrowing 
rate. Generally, the Group uses its incremental borrowing rate as 
the discount rate. 
	
Lease payments include in the measurement of the lease liability 
comprise the following:
• 
fixed payments, including in substance fixed payments; 
•	
variable lease payments that depend on an index or a 
rate, initially measured using the index or rate as at the 
commencement date 
•	
amounts expected to be payable under a residual value 
guarantee and
•	
the exercise price under a purchase option that the Group 
is reasonably certain to exercise, lease payments in an 
optional renewal period if the Group is reasonably certain 
to exercise an extension option, and penalties for early 
termination of a lease unless the Group is reasonably 
certain not to terminate early
	
The lease liability is measured at the amortised cost using the 
effective interest method. It is remeasured when there is change 
in future lease payments arising from a change in index or rate, if 
there is a change in Group’s estimate of the amount expected to 
be payable under a residual value guarantee, if the Group changes 
its assessment of whether it will exercise a purchase, extension or 
termination option or if there is a revised in-substance fixed lease 
payment. When the lease liability is re-measured in this way, a 
corresponding adjustment is made to the carrying amount of the 
right-of-use asset, or is recorded in statement of profit and loss 
if the carrying amount of right-of-use asset has been reduced to 
zero
 
The Group has elected not to recognise right-of-use asset and 
lease liabilities for leases of low-value assets and short-term 
leases. The Group recognises the lease payments associated 
with these leases as an expense in statement of profit and loss 
on a straight-line basis over the lease term.
•	
less any lease incentives receivable, variable lease payment 
that depends on index or a rate, and amount to be paid 
under residual value guarantees. The lease payments are 
discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease or, 
if not readily determinable, the Group uses incremental 
borrowing rates. Lease liabilities are remeasured with a 
corresponding adjustment to the related right of use asset if

.3.11 Income Tax
	
Income tax expense comprises current and deferred tax. It is 
recognized in the statement of profit and loss except to the extent 
that it relates to items recognized directly in other comprehensive 
income or equity, in which case it is recognized in OCI or equity.
	
Current tax comprises the expected tax payable or receivable on 
the taxable income or loss for the year and any adjustment to the 
tax payable in respect of previous years. The amount of current 
tax payable or receivable is the best estimate of the tax amount 
expected to be paid or received that reflects uncertainty related 
to income taxes, if any. It is measured using tax rates enacted or 
substantively enacted at the reporting date.
	
Current tax assets and liabilities are offset only if there is a legally 
enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts, and its 
intended to realize the asset and settle the liability on a net basis 
simultaneously.

Deferred tax is recognized in respect of temporary differences 
between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities for 
financial reporting purposes and the corresponding amounts 
used for taxation purposes. Deferred tax is measured at the 
tax rates that are expected to apply to the period when the 
asset is realised, based on the laws that have been enacted or 
substantively enacted by the reporting date. Deferred tax assets 
and liabilities are offset if there is a legally enforceable right to 
offset current tax liabilities and assets, and they relate to income 
taxes levied by the same tax authority on the same taxable entity, 
or on different tax entities, but they intend to settle current tax 
liabilities and assets on net basis or their tax assets and liabilities 
will be realised simultaneously.
 
Deferred tax is recognized in the statement of profit and loss 
except to the extent that it relates to items recognized directly in 
OCI or equity, in which case it is recognized in OCI or equity.
 
A deferred tax asset is recognized to the extent that it is probable 
that future taxable profits will be available against which the 
temporary difference can be utilized. Deferred tax assets are 
reviewed at each reporting date and are reduced to the extent that 
it is no longer probable that the related tax benefit will be realized.
 
Deferred tax is not recognised for:
•	
temporary differences on the initial recognition of assets or 
liabilities in a transaction that:
	
is not a business combination
	
at the time of transaction (i) affects neither accounting 
nor taxable profit or loss and (ii) does not give rise to 
equal taxable and deductible temporary difference.
•	
temporary differences related to investment in associate to 
the extent that the Group is able to control the timing of the 
reversal of the temporary differences and it is probable that 
they will not reverse in the foreseeable future.
3.12	Earning per share
	
Basic earnings per equity share is computed by dividing the net 
profit or loss attributable to equity shareholders of the Company 
by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding 
during the financial year. The weighted average number of equity 
shares outstanding during the year is adjusted for bonus issue, 
bonus element in a rights issue to existing shareholders, share 
split and reverse share split (consolidation of shares).
	
Diluted earnings per equity share is computed by dividing the net 
profit or loss attributable to equity shareholders of the Company 
by the weighted average number of equity shares considered for 
deriving basic earnings per equity share and also the weighted 
average number of equity shares that could have been issued 
upon conversion of all dilutive potential equity shares.
3.13	Operating segment
	
An operating segment is a component of the Group that engages 
in business activities from which it may earn revenues and 
incur expenses, including revenues and expenses that relate to 
transactions with any of the Group’s other components, and for 
which discrete financial information is available. In accordance 
with Ind AS 108, the operating segments used to present segment 
information are identified on the basis of internal reports used by 
the Group’s management to allocate resources to the segments 
and assess their performance. 
	
The Chairman & Managing Director along with the Board of 
Directors is collectively the Group’s ‘Chief Operating Decision 
Maker’ or ‘CODM’ within the meaning of Ind AS 108. The indicators 
used for internal reporting purposes may evolve in connection 
with performance assessment measures put in place.
3.14	Cash flow statement
 
Cash flows are reported using the indirect method, whereby profit 
or loss for the period is adjusted for the effects of transactions 
of a non-cash nature, any deferrals or accruals of past or future 
operating cash receipts or payments and item of income or 
expenses associated with investing or financing cash flows. The 
cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities of 
the Group are segregated.

d)	
Details of shares issued for consideration other than cash / bonus shares / bought back
	
During the year ended 31 March 2023, the Board of Directors of the Holding Company, at its meeting held on 25 November 2022, approved 
the buyback of equity shares from the open market route through the Indian stock exchanges, amounting to `9,800 (maximum buyback 
size, excluding buyback tax) at a price not exceeding `200 per share (maximum buyback price), subject to approval of the members of the 
Company. The Shareholders approved the proposal for buyback of Equity Shares recommended by its Board of Directors by way of e-voting 
on the postal ballot, the results of which were declared on 30 December 2022. The buyback was offered to all eligible equity shareholders of 
the Company (other than the Promoters, the Promoter Group and Persons in Control of the Company) under the open market route through 
the stock exchange. The buyback of equity shares through the stock exchange commenced on 11 January 2023 and was completed on 
16 March 2023. During this buyback period, the Company purchased and extinguished a total of 6,976,798 equity shares from the stock 
exchange at a weighted average buyback price of `140.45 per equity share comprising 0.78% of the pre buyback paid up equity share capital 
of the Company. The buyback resulted in a cash outflow of `9,798.96 (excluding transaction costs and tax on buyback). The Company funded 
the buyback from its free reserves in accordance with the provisions of Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. In accordance with Section 69 
of the Companies Act, 2013, as at 31 March 2023, the Company had created a ‘Capital Redemption Reserve’ of `69.77 equal to the nominal 
value of the above shares bought back as an appropriation from the general reserve.
	
During the year ended 31 March 2022, the Company had issued 599,113,022 equity shares of `1 each as fully paid-up bonus shares 
representing a ratio of 2 (Two) equity share for every 1 (One) equity share outstanding on the record date.
	
There are no shares issued for consideration other than cash and no shares were bought back during the period of 5 years immediately 
preceding the reporting date, except mentioned above.

41.	 Financial Risk Management
	
The Group’s activities expose it to the followings risks arising from financial instruments:
 
- 
Credit risk
 
- 
Liquidity risk
 
- 
Market risk 
 
 
 
 
 
 
	
This note presents information about the Group’s exposure to each of the above risks, the Group’s objectives, policies and processes for 
measuring and managing risk. 
	
Risk Management framework
	
The Board of Directors (“”the Board””) of the respective companies included in the Group and associate company has overall 
responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the respective company’s risk management framework. The risk management 
policies are established to identify and analyse the risk faced by the respective entities, to set appropriate risk limits and controls 
and to monitor risks and adherence to limits. The respective Board provides written principles for overall risk management, as 
well as policies covering specific areas, such as regulatory risk, compliance risk, technology related risk, IT risk, interest rate risk, 
credit risk, use of derivative financial instruments and non-derivative financial instruments, and investment of excess liquidity. Risk 
management is carried out by an Enterprise Risk Management Committee under risk policy approved by the Board of the Company. 
 
The Audit Committee of respective companies included in the Group and associate company oversees how management monitors 
compliance with risk management policies and procedures, and reviews the adequacy of the risk management framework in relation to 
risks faced by the respective entities.
	
Credit risk	
 
Credit risk is the risk of financial loss to the Group if a customer or counterparty to a financial instrument fails to meet its contractual 
obligations. The carrying amount of the financial assets represents maximum credit exposure.
	
Credit risks on cash and cash equivalents and bank deposits is limited as the Company generally invests in deposits with banks with high 
credit ratings assigned by domestic credit agencies. Investments primarily include investments in mutual fund units, commercial papers, 
market linked debentures, infrastructure investment units, target maturity funds, fixed maturity plans and investment in bonds with fixed 
interest income. The management actively monitors the net asset value of investments in mutual funds, infrastructure investment units, 
interest rate and maturity period of investment in bonds and commercial papers. The Company does not expect the counterparty to fail 
in meeting its obligations. However, investment in target maturity funds, fixed maturity plans, market linked debentures are exposed to 
uncertainties as regards to fulfilment of obligations by counter-party. The Company has not experienced any significant impairment losses 
in respect of any of the investments. In respect of other financial assets including security deposits, the credit risk associated is relatively 
low. Accordingly, no provision for expected credit loss has been provided on such financial assets.
	
Credit risk on trade receivable is also very limited. The Group mitigates its exposure to risks relating to trade receivables from its members 
/ clients by requiring them to comply with the Group’s established financial requirements and criteria for admission as members / clients. 
As a process, the Group collects the amounts from buyer for purchase of power, including transmission and other charges and exchange 
fees on or before the delivery and pays out the amount to seller for sale of power one day after delivery. Further, transmission charges etc. 
are paid to system operator on the next day from the day of trade. Further, the Group also holds and maintain settlement guarantee funds 
for settlement of defaults by any of the members/ clients.

Liquidity risk
 
Liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting the obligations associated with its financial liabilities that are 
settled by payments or another financial asset. The Group’s approach to managing liquidity is to ensure, as far as possible, that it will always 
have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when due, under both normal and stressed conditions, without incurring unacceptable losses 
or risking damage to the Group’s reputation.
 
The Group believes that its liquidity position, comprising total cash (including bank deposits under lien) and short-term investments and 
anticipated future internally generated funds from operations, will enable it to meet its future known obligations in the ordinary course of 
business. However, if liquidity needs were to arise, the Group believes it has access to financing arrangements which would enable it to 
meet its ongoing capital, operating and other liquidity requirements.

Market risk
Market risk is the risk that future cash flows of financial instruments will fluctuate because of change in market price. Market risk 
comprises three types of risk: currency risk, interest rate risk and other price risk. The objective of market risk management is to manage 
and control market risk exposures within acceptable parameters, while optimizing the return.
A. Currency risk
Currency Risk is the risk that the future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of change in foreign exchange rates. 
The Group is not exposed to the effects of fluctuations in the prevailing foreign exchange rates on its financial position and cash flows 
since all financial assets / liabilities are receivable / payable in Indian currency.

49.	 During the year, the Holding Company received a whistle blower complaint relating to alleged conflict of interest and potential diversion of 
business involving certain officials. The Audit Committee has initiated an independent investigation, which remains ongoing as at the date 
of approval of the Consolidated financial statements by the Board of the Holding Company, which do not have a material impact on the 
Consolidated financial statements. Hence, no adjustment has been considered necessary in the Consolidated financial statements.
50.	 The Company had constituted a separate ‘Settlement Guarantee Fund’ (‘SGF’) in respect of the activities carried out in various contracts 
being traded at the exchange platform. The members are required to contribute interest free margin money which forms part of the SGF. 
However, as per CERC order dated 9 October 2018, the Company has to share 70% of the return earned on ‘initial security deposits’ with the 
Members. The margin money is refundable, subject to adjustments, if any. Such fund is also termed as Settlement Guarantee Fund. The 
Cash Margin Money forming part of SGF is `2529.10 (previous year `2,406.48) and same has been disclosed under note 24- Other current 
financial liabilities i.e. `2342.04 (previous year `2,138.30) under Deposits towards Settlement Guarantee Fund and note 19- Other non current 
financial liabilities- Deposits towards Settlement Guarantee Fund i.e. `187.06 (previous year `268.18). These balances have been accounted 
for on amortised cost basis. The Company had also collected non cash portion of the Settlement Fund comprising collateral such as bank 
guarantees, received from the members amounting to `25.00 (previous year `65.00) which does not form part of the Balance Sheet.  
51.	 The Company receives trading margin deposits from the members corresponding to their average trading volume during last 7 days. Trading 
margin money is refundable, subject to adjustments, if any. The Cash Margin Money forming part of trading margin deposits is `17,126.35 
(previous year `16,419.77) and same has been disclosed under note 24 - Other current financial liabilities. The Company has also collected 
non cash portion of the trading margin deposits comprising collateral such as bank guarantees, received from the members amounting to 
`3,935.00 (previous year `2,230.00) which does not form part of the Balance Sheet.
52. The Government of India has enacted the following labour codes, which subsume and replace multiple existing labour laws: Code on Wages, 
2019, Industrial Relations Code, 2020, Code on Social Security, 2020, Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. The 
implementation of the labour codes is subject to issuance of the relevant rules and notifications by the Central and State Governments. 
The Company has undertaken an assessment of the potential impact of these labour codes on its financial statements, including employee 
benefits, social security contributions and related compliances. Based on the assessment carried out and considering the current status 
of implementation, the Company does not expect a material impact on its financial information at the time of adoption. The Company will 
continue to monitor developments in this regard and will appropriately evaluate and account for the impact, if any, in the period in which the 
labour codes become effective.
53. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (“CERC”) vide its Suo Motu Order dated July 23, 2025, proposing the process for implementation 
of market coupling for the Day Ahead Market (DAM) of power exchanges by January 2026. The Company challenged the aforesaid CERC 
order before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL). The Hon’ble APTEL, vide its order held that the Company is not a “person aggrieved” 
at this stage, as market coupling can be implemented only once the separate Regulations are framed by the CERC. Against the Hon’ble APTEL 
order, the Company has filed a civil appeal before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India. Subsequently, on April 17, 2026, CERC issued the draft 
CERC (Power Market) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026, proposing amendments to the existing CERC (Power Market) Regulations, 
2021 for public consultation.

As per IT Act, dividends paid or distributed by 
the Company are taxable in the hands of the 
shareholders. Accordingly, companies are 
required to deduct tax at source from 
dividends paid to shareholders. 
 
The rate of deduction of tax depends on: 
a) Residential status of the shareholder. 
b) Valid tax registration (PAN or equivalent 
taxpayer identification) 
c) The documents/declarations submitted 
by the shareholder and accepted by the 
Company. 
 
For resident individual shareholders: 
 
a. As per section 393(1) [Table: Sr. No. 7] of 
the IT Act, any domestic company making 
payment to a resident shareholder shall 
deduct tax 10% at the time of payment of 
dividend to shareholder if it exceeds 
Rs.10,000 and who has provided valid 
PAN. However, on submission of any 
lower withholding tax certificate under 
provision of the Act for Tax Year 2026-27, 
the withholding tax shall be at the rate 
mentioned in the certificate issued by the 
Authority. 
b. As per section 393(4) [Table: Sr. No. 10], 
no tax shall be deducted if the amount or 
aggregate of amounts of such dividend 
distributed or paid or likely to be 
distributed or paid during the tax year 
does not exceed Rs.10,000 and the 
dividend is paid in any mode other than in 
cash. 
c. As per section 393(6) of the IT Act, if 
shareholder 
provides 
duly 
filed 
declaration in Form 121 for relevant tax 
year (T.Y. 2026-27) complete in all

A RESILIENT AND FUTURE-READY POWER SECTOR
Electricity is one of the key enablers of India’s economic transformation. As the nation 
advances towards becoming a global manufacturing and digital powerhouse, the power 
sector continues to evolve with greater scale, reliability and technological integration. 
Over the past decade, the country’s power sector 
ecosystem has undergone remarkable transition - from 
addressing shortages and expanding access to building 
a modern, resilient and future-ready energy infrastructure 
- capable of supporting sustained economic growth. 
India’s power demand trajectory reflects the pace 
of the country’s development. Rapid urbanisation, 
rising industrial activity, infrastructure expansion and 
increasing digital adoption are continuously driving 
electricity consumption upward. During FY’26, India 
successfully met a peak power demand of 245 GW while 
reducing power shortages to just 0.03%, which marks 
a substantial improvement from 4.2% in FY’14. This 
transformation highlights the strengthening generation 
capacity, transmission networks and grid management 
systems across the country.
One of the most significant achievements of the sector 
has been the expansion of electricity access across 
India.  The world’s largest synchronous national grid now 
exceeds 5 lakh circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission 
lines. Through large-scale rural electrification and last-
mile connectivity initiatives, electricity today r

eaches 
nearly every village and household in the country. Flagship 
programmes such as Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti 
Yojana (DDUGJY), Integrated Power Development Scheme 
(IPDS) and Saubhagya accelerated the creation of modern 
distribution infrastructure and enabled electricity access 
for nearly 30 million households. Improved supply 
reliability has positively impacted education, healthcare, 
agriculture and small enterprises, particularly in rural and 
semi-urban India.
The sector’s evolution is also visible in the steady 
improvement in quality and availability of power supply. 
Average daily power supply in rural India has increased 
substantially over the last decade, while urban areas 
continue to witness near-round-the-clock availability. 
Per capita electricity consumption in India has also 
risen to 1,460 kilowatt-hours in FY’25, registering an

India’s

has 
further

sources constituted over 50% of the country’s installed

clean energy transition, reflecting the growing maturity of 
the country’s renewable energy ecosystem and its ability 
to integrate clean energy into the national grid.
Continued investments in transmission infrastructure 
are ensuring that growing renewable capacity can be 
efficiently integrated and delivered across regions. The 
National Electricity Plan 2023–2032 outlines a strong 
roadmap for future-ready transmission systems, inter-
regional connectivity and grid expansion to support rising 
electricity demand and emerging energy applications.
The financial and operational performance of distribution 
utilities has also shown notable improvement. AT&C 
losses declined to 15% in FY’25 from 16% in FY’24, while 
the narrowing of the ACS-ARR gap and improved payment 
discipline across the value chain reflect the impact 
of sustained reforms and operational strengthening. 
Timely payments to generators and a growing focus on 
power procurement optimisation further underscore the 
sector’s transition towards greater financial discipline 
and operational efficiency. These developments are 
creating a healthier and more sustainable ecosystem for 
long-term sectoral growth.
As India’s economy continues to expand, electricity 
will remain central to industrial competitiveness, digital 
growth, urban development and sustainability ambitions. 
Emerging sectors such as electric mobility, data centres, 
green hydrogen and advanced manufacturing are 
expected to further accelerate demand for reliable and 
clean power.
In this evolving landscape, the Indian Energy Exchange 
(IEX) endeavors to remain at the forefront of technology-
enabled and market-driven solutions in ensuring

THE SHIFT TO SMARTER POWER PROCUREMENT
State power utilities in the country are steadily transforming how they procure electricity 
and the shift is already evident in the numbers. Across India, distribution companies 
are moving beyond traditional methods and involving power exchanges into their core 
supply planning processes. What was once an option to address short-term deficits 
or unexpected demand has evolved into a strategic procurement channel, guided by 
data-driven decision-making. On the strength of leveraging price signals, generation 
economics, and time-of-day demand patterns, utilities are adopting a more dynamic 
and informed approach to sourcing power.
This transformation is reshaping three critical elements 
of DISCOM operations: the timing of procurement 
decisions, the scheduling of State-allocated generation, 
and the daily optimisation of supply-demand balance. 
States such as Uttarakhand, West Bengal, and Punjab 
exemplify this shift, having embedded market-based 
procurement as a central pillar of their operational 
strategy.
In Punjab, for instance, long-term PPAs had kept the 
load curve largely flat, but the State discom has shifted 
significant demand to daytime hours to tap surplus, low-
cost solar power. By actively tracking price trends and 
increasing participation in DAM, RTM, and the Green 
Day-Ahead Market on IEX, the State discom optimized 
costs, improved reliability, and supported sustainability 
goals, all reflected in a 50% CAGR in exchange purchases

where average prices touched `2.34/unit and `2.51/

Uttarakhand has also integrated power exchanges into 
routine supply planning, using data-driven procurement 
and saved over `160 crore in FY’26, while also earning 
`125 crore from REC sales. Initially procuring via the

State discom shifted to a diversified strategy leveraging 
exchange products to lower costs. It sourced nearly

beyond its RPO needs which it monetized by selling 35 
lakh RECs on exchanges at an average price of `350 per 
REC, generating `125 crore in additional revenue.

signals a lasting change in procurement strategy. Data 
from multiple regions shows measurable gains: lower 
purchase costs, better demand–supply balance and 
new revenue streams from surplus power. As renewable 
capacity continues to expand and hourly price variation 
becomes sharper, States that actively respond to market 
signals are likely to widen their financial advantage. 
Exchange-led procurement is therefore not just a short-
term tactic, it is becoming a defining feature of how 
India’s power system is planned and managed.

GREEN MARKETS: TECHNOLOGY ENABLING A 
SUSTAINABLE ENERGY FUTURE
India’s energy transition is no longer a vision for the future, it is a transition unfolding at a 
rapid pace. With non-fossil sources accounting for half of the country’s installed power 
capacity, the nation has entered a defining decade in its journey towards achieving its 
2030 climate commitments and 2070 commitment of net-zero emissions. Renewable 
energy has moved beyond incremental growth to become a fundamental pillar of India’s 
power system, delivering lower energy costs, reducing dependence on imported fuels, 
and reshaping electricity markets. 
As this transition gathers momentum, the challenge is 
no longer limited to adding renewable capacity. The next 
phase lies in integrating renewable energy efficiently 
into the grid. The growing share of solar and wind 
generation has introduced a new level of complexity to 
system operations. Their inherent variability has led to 
larger intra-day forecast deviations, sharper net-load 
ramps and more frequent real-time imbalances, making 
flexibility and responsive market mechanisms essential 
for maintaining grid reliability.
At IEX, we believe that well-designed markets are central 
to enabling this transformation. Over the years, we 
have continuously expanded our market architecture 
to address the evolving needs of India’s power sector, 
creating innovative products that enhance flexibility, 
improve price discovery and accelerate renewable 
energy adoption.
A significant milestone in this journey has been the 
creation of India’s first Green Market through the Green 
Day-Ahead Market (G-DAM) and the Green Term-Ahead 
Market (G-TAM). IEX has built transparent, market-
based avenues for energy procurement and trading. 
These products empower renewable-rich States to 
monetise surplus green power beyond their compliance 
obligations while enabling generators to adopt flexible 
procurement strategies, ranging from hybrid market-
PPA struc

tures to fully market-based models. In doing 
so, IEX is strengthening the economic case for renewable 
energy while supporting the sustainability ambitions of 
both corporates and the nation at large.

The market response has been equally encouraging. As 
renewable generation has increased, green power prices 
have become increasingly competitive, encouraging 
greater participation in the Green Market. This has 
translated into strong growth in traded volumes across 
the Green Market, registering 23% YoY growth, with the 
Green Market accounting for nearly 8% of the electricity 
volume traded on the Exchange in FY’26. The increasing 
contribution of green market products to IEX’s overall 
product mix reflects the growing confidence of market 
participants in transparent, exchange-based renewable 
power procurement.
Alongside the Green Market, the Real-Time Market (RTM) 
has emerged as an indispensable pillar of renewable 
integration. As renewable penetration increases, balancing 
demand and supply closer to delivery has become critical. 
RTM enables market participants to respond to real-time 
system conditions through transparent price signals, 
improving economic dispatch, correcting imbalances 
efficiently and facilitating secure integration of renewable 
energy. For DISCOMs, particularly in renewable-rich states 
such as Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Andhra 
Pradesh, RTM has become a valuable tool for portfolio 
optimisation and reducing renewable energy curtailment 
by providing an efficient platform to sell surplus power. 
Reflecting its growing relevance and operational value, 
the RTM segment has recorded a five-year CAGR of 42% 
and in FY’26 accounted for 34% of the total electricity 
traded volume on IEX.
Beyond electricity trading, IEX is also enabling India’s 
sustainability ambitions through RECs and International 
Renewable Certificates (I-REC). The

REC market, which 
commenced trading on power exchanges in 2011, has 
also played a pivotal role in enabling obligated entities 
to meet their Renewable Consumption Obligation 
(RCO) requirements while facilitating India’s broader 
decarbonisation 
journey. 
Going 
beyond 
national 
boundaries, through ICX, India’s first I-REC(E) issuer 
approved by the I-TRACK Foundation, ICX aims to make 
a global impact on the voluntary carbon market.
The evolution of India’s energy markets is also creating 
new opportunities beyond electricity trading. Battery 
Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are beginning to reshape 
system flexibility, with large-scale additions and declining 
discovered tariffs enabling merchant-based BESS 
transactions on the IEX. At the same time, the emerging 
regulatory framework for Carbon Credit Certificates is 
laying the foundation for transparent, market-based 
carbon trading, extending the principles of efficient price 
discovery from electricity to emissions management.
As clean energy adoption accelerates across industries, 
market-based mechanisms will play an increasingly 
strategic role in enabling India’s path to a low-carbon 
economy. Guided by innovation, transparency and 
efficiency, IEX remains committed to building markets 
that not only facilitate energy transition but also create 
enduring value for every stakeholder.
This commitment extends beyond markets. As India’s 
first carbon-neutral power exchange for three years 
running, IEX continues to demonstrate that sustainability 
and business growth can progress together, supporting 
the nation’s transition towards a cleaner, more resilient 
and future-ready energy ecosystem.

foundation of technology, innovation and customer centricity.

participants while strengthening its position as India’s leading 
electricity marketplace. This commitment to innovation and 
operational excellence has enabled IEX to remain agile in 
a rapidly evolving energy landscape. As the organisation 
matured, so did its vision. The expertise gained from developing 
and scaling India’s largest electricity exchange, encompassing

WHAT IS I-REC(E)?
The International Renewable Energy Certificate for Electricity 
[I-REC(E)] is a tradable Energy Attribute Certificate (EAC) 
that conveys verified information about the production 
of one megawatt-hour (1 MWh) of electricity such as its 
source, production facility, and its capacity. Accredited by the 
International Tracking Standard Foundation, I-REC(E) enables 
electricity users wo

rldwide to credibly report renewable

and voluntary initiatives. By procuring I-REC(E), companies 
can claim renewable energy usage, reduce Scope 2 emissions,

the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)—demonstrating 
measurable progress toward net-zero and sustainability goals.

Building on IEX’s deep expertise in the Indian power sector, ICX 
has brought strong governance and credibility to the voluntary 
I-REC(E) market by tailoring international frameworks to India’s

and the I-REC(E) Code, ICX has instituted rigorous processes 
to ensure integrity, transparency, and the elimination of double 
counting. This includes conducting detailed analyses of Central 
and State regulations, embedding regulatory checks into device 
registration and certificate issuance, and proactively addressing 
challenges related to Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPOs). 
Additionally, ICX has streamlined the identification and 
treatment of banking quantum as per State-specific rules, 
ensuring robust compliance. Through these measures, ICX has 
added substantial value as the local I-REC(E) Issuer, fostering

renewable energy certificate ecosystem. This has resulted in

access to I-REC(E), ICX has provided Indian corporates with 
the same credibility and recognition enjoyed by their peers 
globally. This international parity has not only strengthened 
ESG disclosures but also enhanced investor confidence in the 
country’s corporate sustainability journey.

INDIAN COAL EXCHANGE: BUILDING THE 
MARKET ARCHITECTURE FOR INDIA’S COAL 
ECONOMY
Earlier in 2026, IEX incorporated Indian Coal Exchange to 
support the next phase of

India’s Coal Economy.
For decades, India’s coal sector is focused on increasing 
domestic production to meet the country’s growing energy 
demand. Today, the challenge is evolving to ensure that coal 
production is discovered, priced, traded and allocated more 
efficiently. India produced a little over 1.0 billion tonnes of coal 
in FY’26 and production is expected to reach 1.5 billion tonnes

tonnes by FY’35.

transparency and price discovery are becoming as important as

building transparent and efficient marketplaces to India’s coal

CREATING A MARKET FOR A MULTI-SELLER 
COAL ECONOMY
Policy reforms over the past few years have transformed the 
structure of the coal market. Commercial coal mining has 
removed the end use restrictions encouraging wider private 
participation. While captive mines were permitted to sell up to 
50% of their production in the open market. Consequently, Coal 
India’s share of domestic production has declined from around 
80% in FY’22 to 74% in FY’26, while captive and commercial 
mines now contribute 20% and SCCL accounts for 6%. 
Although Coal India sold around 11% of its production through

captive and commercial mines continues to be traded through 
bilateral arrangements. As tradable volumes increase, a multi-

sellers.

The notification of the Coal Exchange Rules, 2026, following 
amendments to the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, has established the regulatory framework for 
exchange-based coal trading.

transparent domestic benchmark prices, improve procurement 
efficiency and strengthen market visibility across the coal value 
chain. Beyond facilitating transactions, it can support better 
allocation of domestic coal, improve market competitiveness 
and contribute to more efficient utilisation of the country’s 
growing coal resources.

commitment to building the market infrastructure needed for 
India’s evolving energy landscape. As the coal sector becomes 
larger, more competitive and increasingly market-driven, IEX 
is poised to support the next phase of India’s coal economy 
through greater transparency, efficiency and robust price 
discovery.

DIVERSIFICATION: BUILDING INDIA’S MULTI-MARKET ENERGY 
GROUP
IEX’s vision extends well beyond electricity. Our diversification 
agenda is systematically transforming IEX into India’s leading 
multi-market energy group, spanning gas, carbon, and now 
coal.
The Indian Gas Exchange (IGX) completed five years of 
operations in FY’26 and continues to strengthen its position 
as India’s premier gas exchange. Representing close to 3% of 
India’s total gas consumption and 20% of the spot market, IGX 
traded 76.8 million MMBtu in FY’26, a 28% year-on-year growth, 
driven by demand from domestic producers, the power sector, 
and city gas distribution companies. IGX achieved a Profit 
After Tax of `41.9 Crore, 35% higher than the previous year, 
reflecting both operational scale and growing market adoption.

PNGRB regulations, it has to bring it holding down to 25%. IGX 
has initiated its IPO process. The Offer comprises an offer for 
sale of up to 22.28% equity shares by IEX, and remains subject 
to receipt of applicable approvals, market conditions, and other 
relevant considerations. The IPO aims to unlock further value 
for the gas market and for IEX shareholders.
Our wholly owned subsidiary, ICX, is gaining significant traction 
as India’s only accredited International Renewable Energy 
Certificate (I-REC) issuer. In FY’26, ICX issued 179 lakh I-RECs, 
highlighting a growth of over 200% compared with the previous 
year, with revenue rising to `7.7 Crore. As India’s voluntary 
carbon and clean energy markets mature, ICX is positioned 
to play an expanding role in h

elping organisations meet their 
global sustainability commitments.

Exchange, our Board has accorded in-principle approval to 
explore this opportunity, and we have registered a wholly

With the Final Rules requiring existing e-auction platforms 
to transition to Coal Exchange trading within six months of 
operationalization, the opportunity size in the very first year 
itself could be about 100 million tonnes. Additionally, we are 
exploring the opportunity to set up a Minerals Exchange as 
another area of potential growth.

THE ROAD AHEAD: A FUTURE OF OPPORTUNITY
The long-term outlook for India’s power sector is compelling. 
With electricity demand projected by CEA to approach 2,700 
billion units and peak demand of 388 GW by FY’32 and GDP 
growing at 7–8% per annum, the coming decade will demand 
significant investment in generation, transmission, storage, and 
market infrastructure. Power exchanges will be at the center 
of this transition. Over the next few years, several structural 
growth opportunities will shape our journey:
1.	 Electrification of the Economy — Rising industrialisation, the 
expansion of railways and metro networks, and the broad-
based shift from fossil fuels to electricity across sectors 
are structurally increasing India’s electricity intensity. As 
the economy electrifies, power demand will grow well 
beyond historical patterns, creating sustained headroom 
for exchange-based procurement by DISCOMs, industries, 
and open-access consumers.

2.	 Data Centres and the AI Economy — India is witnessing 
a rapid surge in data centre capacity, driven by the digital

operators scale up in India, their demand for green power 
through market mechanisms will grow substantially.
3.	 Electric Vehicles and Charging Infrastructure — India’s EV 
transition is gaining momentum, and with it comes a new, 
distributed source of electricity demand. As EV penetration 
rises across personal, commercial, and public transport 
segments, charging infrastructure will require grid-scale 
power, with much of it optimally procured through market 
platforms. Exchanges can play a key role in enabling cost-
effective, time-of-day optimised power procurement for 
charging operators, and in integrating vehicle-to-grid 
capabilities as the ecosystem matures.
4.	 Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) — Large-scale 
BESS additions, with over 43 GWh supported through VGF 
mechanism and rapid decline of discovered tariffs, will 
play a transformative role in the market. BESS will absorb 
surplus solar generation during the day and deliver power 
during peak evening and morning hours, directly boosting 
exchange-cleared volumes. FY’26 marked the first 
merchant BESS trades on IEX, from Juniper Green Energy, 
followed by ACME Solar and Adani Green, bringing a new 
class of market participants and validating the storage 
arbitrage model.
5.	 New Market Mechanisms — The emergence of VPPAs, 
Contract-for-Difference, electricity derivatives, and Firm and 
Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) tenders will deepen 
market liquidity and broaden participation. The structural 
over-sizing inherent in FDRE projects will generate surplus 
generation that flows to exchanges, boosting both buy and 
sell liquidity. Electricity derivatives, now live on MCX and 
NSE, are expected to deepen spot market participation by 
enabling participants to hedge price risk.
6.	 Green Markets : Growing renewable generation and 
competitive green power prices have fueled participation 
in the Green Market. The Green

consequently recorded a three-year CAGR of over 50% and

opportunity for both compliance and voluntary procurement
7.	 Carbon  Markets — The Carbon Credit Certificate market, 
expected to commence trading by FY’27, represents a 
significant new revenue stream for IEX. With emission 
intensity reduction targets now notified for seven industrial 
sectors and compliance timelines approaching, obligated 
entities will need a transparent, market-based platform 
for carbon credit trading, a role IEX is uniquely positioned 
to fulfil through its exchange infrastructure and regulatory 
standing. 
8.	 Innovative RE Tendering and P2P Markets — The shift from 
plain-vanilla solar and wind tenders to firm and dispatchable 
models such as FDRE and RTC is creating new sell-side 
liquidity on exchanges. In parallel, the rise of rooftop solar, 
with installed capacity now reached 30 GW, and the push by 
states such as Karnataka, Delhi, and Uttar Pradesh towards 
peer-to-peer trading frameworks signal the emergence of a 
local energy market ecosystem where exchanges will play a 
central enabling role.

INDIA’S POWER SECTOR
Countrywide electricity demand in FY’26 was 1,707 BUs, a 
marginal year-on-year increase of approximately 1%, reflecting 
a moderation in the pace of demand growth over FY’25. 
The slowdown was primarily driven by an early onset of the 
Southwest monsoon in May 2025, which reduced cooling needs 
and agricultural pump usage, compressing cooling-degree 
days significantly. Nevertheless, India’s lo

ng-run power demand 
drivers of rising income levels, rapid urbanisation, government 
electrification initiatives, expanding manufacturing, and electric 
vehicle adoption remain firmly intact. 
The power sector continued its rapid structural transformation 
in FY’26 with record-breaking capacity addition. India’s total 
installed generation capacity reached 533 GW as on 31st 
March 2026, an addition of 58 GW in a single year, the highest-
ever annual increment. India’s renewable installed capacity 
(excluding large hydro) crossed 230 GW, driven by record 
solar additions. A total of 55 GW of non-fossil capacity was 
added, the highest ever in a single year. Solar capacity surged 
to approximately 150 GW, while wind capacity rose to 57 GW. 
Total non-fossil capacity as on 31st March 2026 stood at 283 
GW (including large hydro and nuclear).Renewables (including 
large hydro) now account for approximately 53% of total 
installed capacity, a milestone. During this fiscal, India achieved 
50% non-fossil installed capacity nearly five years ahead of its 
2030 target.

TRANSMISSION
The nation’s regional grids remain seamlessly interconnected 
under the ‘One Nation One Grid One Frequency’ framework. The 
inter-regional capacity has increased by more than 75% since 
2014, reflecting sustained investment in grid infrastructure. 
This integrated system enables efficient electricity distribution 
across all regions, strengthening the reliability and resilience 
of the entire power network. As of March 31st, 2026, India’s 
interregional transmission capacity of the National Grid stood at 
over 120 GW, with transmission line length and transformation 
capacity continuing to expand significantly. Indi

a’s national 
transmission network has crossed a major milestone 
exceeding 5 lakh circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission lines 
and reaching a total transformation capacity of 1,407 gigavolt 
amperes (GVA). By reinforcing both generation and networks 
simultaneously, India has laid the foundation for a power sector 
that can support growth not just today, but well into the future. 
The National Electricity Plan (2023–2032) for Central and State 
transmission systems has also been finalised to meet the 
projected peak demand by 2032 and involves an estimated

ECONOMIC EXPANSION AND POWER MARKETS
Industrial Growth and Urbanisation
Industrial growth and urbanisation remain key elements in 
India’s economic development and ongoing power sector 
transformation. The Government’s thrust on Atmanirbhar Bharat 
and policy measures to position India as the cornerstone of 
the China Plus One strategy for global businesses augmented 
exports and domestic productive capacities in FY’26. This was 
despite global trade uncertainties. These policy measures 
continue to drive increased electricity demand from the 
manufacturing sectors.
India has achieved notable strides in urbanisation. It is 
projected that by 2030, over 40% of India’s population will be 
living in cities. Although these cities occupy only about 3% 
of the country’s total land area, they remarkably

generate 
60% of India’s GDP. India’s rapid urbanisation is projected to 
significantly increase energy consumption. Further, expected 
electricity demand from the growth of AI and data centres is 
also factored into the planning process of the government as it 
reinforces long-term demand projections. This AI growth boom 
is driven by cloud adoption, data localization mandates, and 
localized Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) workloads. As per 
the Ministry of Power, electricity demand from data centres is 
estimated to touch nearly 14 GW by FY’32. The strong growth 
in data centre demand is likely to trigger parallel demand for up 
to 50 GW of renewable energy. In the near term power demand 
is expected to touch almost 2,700 BUs with a peak demand of 
388 GW by FY’32.
Demand and Supply
According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), all India 
energy consumption reached approximately 1,707 Billion Units 
(BU) in FY’26, representing a year-on-year growth of about 1.1% 
from 1,692 BU in FY’25. The moderation in demand growth 
was primarily driven by an early onset of the monsoon in May 
2025, which reduced cooling degree days by more than 7% 
compared to 2024, with a 12% decline in June alone, a month 
which typically accounts for about 15% of annual demand. The 
peak demand met during the summer in FY’26 was 242 GW 
recorded in June 2025, while in June FY’25 peak demand stood 
at 245 GW.
The Northern Region remained the largest contributor to 
demand, though due to weather related events growth rates 
varied significantly across regions in FY’26. Key States such 
as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Uttar 
Pradesh recorded the highest peak demand levels.

OUTLOOK
In FY’26, India demonstrated remarkable resilience in navigating 
a complex global environment characterised by geopolitical 
tensions, evolving trade policies, and climate-linked demand 
volatility. India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals, robust 
private consumption, fiscal consolidation, and sustained public 
capex continue to underpin healthy power demand growth over 
the medium term. With India firmly on its trajectory to remain 
the world’s fastest-growing major economy, the power market 
is well-positioned to capitalise on annual incremental demand 
of nearly 100 BUs projected through 2030. The accelerating 
shift towards renewables, rising need for market-based storage 
dispatch supported by the government’s push on addition of 
BESS and PSP, introduction of newer market mechanisms, 
the structural load shifts in agriculture, and expansion of open 
access participation provide sustained growth levers for power 
market development.

The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) REC 
Regulations 2022, which went into effect from December 
5th, 2022 and were fully implemented in FY’24, continued to

are traded on exchanges twice a month, providing consumers 
competitive rates.

transactions and propose measures for further increasing 
auction frequency beyond the current twice-a-month schedule, 
with stakeholder consultations ongoing. REC fungibility and 
elimination of the floor price have enhanced market liquidity, 
with REC inventory levels close to 3.9 crore certificates at the 
close of FY’26.

of 187.20 lakh (18.72 million) RECs traded, representing nearly 
18.72 BUs of electricity, higher by 5% on a year-on-year basis.

the growing significance of RECs in promoting renewable

CORE BUSINESS GROWTH
Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) has been actively working to 
deepen and diversify the short-term power market while 
expanding its share within this segment. Over the years, IEX 
has continuously enhanced market flexibility by introducing 
innovative products and extending contract tenures to better 
meet the evolving requirements of market participants. To 
further strengthen the market and provide participants with 
greater flexibility in procurement and portfolio management, 
IEX has filed petitions with the Hon’ble CERC seeking approvals 
on new segments that would deepen power markets and 
strengthen the foundation for sustainable growth and 
innovation. Through continuous market development, product 
innovation, and the introduction of new market mechanisms. 
IEX aims to create a more robust, efficient, and future-ready 
electricity market ecosystem. The following areas serve as the 
cornerstone of our vision and drive our core business growth:
•	 Power Procurement Optimisation by Discoms
	 With over 90 distribution companies currently registered, 
IEX works closely with these utilities to reduce their power 
procurement expenses by leveraging cost-competitive 
merit order scheduling. The exchange assists utilities in 
both short-term bilateral contracts and long-term Power 
Purchase Agreements (PPAs) by identifying opportunities to 
replace expensive power with more affordable alternatives 
available on its platform. This strategy enables distribution 
companies to realize substantial cost savings. Furthermore, 
IEX actively supports these utilities through ongoing 
capacity-building and educational programs, ensuring they 
are well-equipped to maximize the value and efficiency of 
their power procurement activities.
•	 Growing Ope

n Access Procurement  
	 Electricity remains one of the most significant cost 
components for industries. In energy-intensive sectors such 
as cement, metals, automobiles, chemicals and paper, power 
procurement can account for nearly 50% of operating costs. 
Power exchanges provide open-access consumers with the 
flexibility to supplement their power requirements based on 
prevailing market conditions. Transparent price discovery and 
a range of short-duration products allow consumers to align 
procurement decisions with production schedules, demand 
patterns and generation availability. Over 5,900 commercial 
and industrial consumers across India utilise IEX’s platform 
to procure competitively priced power. These prices provided 
an opportunity for open-access consumers to optimize their 
power procurement costs throughout the year in FY’26, 
rather than being solely dependent on discom procurement. 
It also provided an opportunity to replace costlier power from 
captive generation with more competitively priced power 
available through the exchange. Reflecting this growing 
value proposition, participation by open-access consumers 
on power exchanges has increased significantly, with traded 
volumes growing by over 50% year-on-year Several States 
are also encouraging renewable energy procurement through 
Green Markets on power exchanges supported policies that 
provide exemptions from additional surcharge. The Ministry 
of Power over the last few years has introduced significant 
amendments to Electricity Rules, enabling large industrial 
users to establish their own transmission lines and grid 
connections without requiring a license. To further promote 
open access, IEX actively engages with potential consumers, 
raises awareness and advocates for policy and regulatory 
reforms at both the Central and State levels. Our efforts 
aim to address systemic challenges and remove tariff and 
non-tariff barriers, ensuring seamless access to competitive 
power procure

ment.

a)	 Green Real Time Market (G-RTM) and TAM-11 Month: As 
part of our strategy to deepen and diversify the short-term 
power market, IEX has filed petitions with the Hon’ble CERC 
for the introduction of the Green Real-Time Market (G-RTM) 
and the extension of Term-Ahead Market (TAM) contracts 
from the current 90 days to up to 11 months. While G-RTM 
will enable efficient real-time trading of renewable energy 
through Green-tagged contracts, supporting renewable

flexibility, planning certainty, and procurement options. 
Together, these initiatives are aimed at enhancing market 
efficiency, expanding customer choice, and supporting 
India’s evolving power sector requirements. We continue to 
await approval from the CERC on both these petitions.

mechanism to procure electricity specifically during 
peak consumption periods, thereby helping discoms and 
consumers manage demand fluctuations more effectively. 
The proposed market segment would support development 
of merchant storage capacity and thereby enhance grid 
reliability, improve resource optimization, and provide

Battery Energy Storage Systems
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) remain a cornerstone 
of India’s clean energy transition, enabling seamless integration 
of renewable power into the national grid. In FY’24, the 
Ministry of Power i

ntroduced the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) 
mechanism to catalyse 4,000 MWh of BESS capacity, which 
was later expanded to 13,200 GWh in response to falling costs. 
Building on the success of Tranche I, the Ministry of Power 
launched VGF Tranche II with a target of 30,000 MWh, marking 
a significant scale up. By March FY’26, tenders totalling 43,000 
MWh had been floated, with nearly 40,000 MWh successfully 
awarded and the rest were in the tendering process stage. The 
pace of tender clearances has emerged as a clear reflection

BESS plays a dual role in the evolving energy landscape by 
storing surplus solar generation during solar hours (day-time) 
and dispatching electricity during evening peaks, while also 
stabilizing the grid during periods of high renewable penetration. 
One of the key operational models under consideration is the 
charge and discharge through power exchanges, where current 
prices range between `2.0–`2.5 per unit during solar hours and 
`5–`7 per unit in the evening, offering a compelling arbitrage 
opportunity for BESS operators. For an ISTS connected BESS 
project for 2-hrs BESS including ISTS losses and Round-trip 
efficiency (RtE), the annual arbitrage is around `4.81/unit 
(with 545 annual cycles) and for a 4-hrs BESS project the 
annual arbitrage is around `3.91/unit (with 484 annual cycles). 
With falling discovered tariffs, expectations of further cost 
reductions, and expanding participation in ancillary services, 
BESS has firmly established itself as a commercially viable and 
strategically essential component of India’s energy ecosystem.

Deepening India’s green power markets is essential to reduce

replacing the earlier Solar, Non-Solar, and Hydro classifications 
with four new categories — Wind, Hydro, Distributed Renewable

the Ministry of Power’s revised Renewable Consumption 
Obligation (RCO) notification of September 2025. The revised 
framework applies across IEX’s full suite of green market 
products, including the Green Day Ahead Market (G-DAM), 
Green Day Ahead Contingency (G-DAC), Green Intra-Day 
Contracts, and Green Daily, Weekly, and Monthly Contracts, in 
effect, strengthening the alignment between exchange-traded 
green power and India’s evolving clean energy compliance 
architecture.
With regards Virtual Power Purchase Agreement (VPPA), FY’26 
marked a landmark regulatory milestone. CERC finalised the 
VPPA Guidelines through a notification dated December 24, 
2025, published in the Gazette on January 28, 2026, providing 
a structured and legally certain pathway for designated 
consumers and corporates to procure renewable energy 
attributes without the need for physical power delivery. Under 
this framework, the renewable energy generator sells power 
independently on exchanges such as IEX, while the difference 
between the market-discovered price and the pre-agreed 
reference price is settled bilaterally  with Renewable Energy 
Certificates (RECs) transferred to the consumer to enable 
Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO) compliance.
These guidelines mark a significant milestone in India’s journey 
towards energy transition, providing a credible and structured 
instrument for corporates to meet their green procurement 
goals.  The VPPA model is posed to gain signific

ant traction 
among Commercial & Industrial (C&I) consumers as corporates 
accelerate their decarbonisation commitments while retaining 
operational flexibility in power scheduling. Beyond compliance, 
VPPAs are increasingly being recognised as an effective long-
term price hedging instrument for C&I customers, offering 
revenue certainty to RE developers while insulating buyers from 
market price volatility.

that better reflect the true value of distributed generation.
P2P electricity trading has been gaining traction globally, driven 
by the proliferation of prosumers-households and entities 
that both generate and consume energy. India is witnessing 
encouraging momentum on this front. In February 2026, REC 
Limited, the nodal agency for the India Energy Stack under the 
Ministry of Power showcased the first-ever live demonstration 
of a peer-to-peer decentralised energy transaction under 
the India Energy Stack (IES) framework, underscoring the 
Government’s commitment to enabling technology-driven 
local energy markets. Under the India Energy Stack, consumers 
generating renewable energy through rooftop solar systems will 
be able to trade surplus electricity with other users, including 
across State borders, operating on a secure, trust-based digital 
framework to ensure transactions are verifiable and scalable.
The P2P initiative is currently being positioned as a policy 
sandbox, with its immediate objective being digital validation 
in terms of testing identity management, smart meter data 
exchange, interoperable APIs, price discovery tools, billing 
integration, and settlement systems within a controlled 
environment. The pilot focuses primarily on rooftop solar 
prosumers which includes residential, commercial, and 
institutional consumers equipped with smart meters at 
distribution voltage levels.
States such as Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, and Delhi have taken 
the lead in issuing guidelines and regulations to govern and 
promote P2P trading, while others such as Assam and Odisha 
are advancing regulatory frameworks to support decentralized 
energy markets. As rooftop solar capacities continue to 
scale under the PM Surya Ghar scheme, it is expected that 
more States will progressively establish enabling regulatory 
frameworks, paving the way for a vibrant, decentralised

energy 
market ecosystem in India.
Carbon Market
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) has undergone 
significant evolution, emerging as the mainstay of India’s 
market-based climate action framework. Following its 2023 
amendment to include the Offset Mechanism, the scheme 
now encompasses both obligated entities with binding targets 
and non-obligated entities that may voluntarily participate 
by purchasing Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) to fulfil their 
sustainability commitments.
The CCTS operates as an intensity-based baseline-and-credit 
system, with targets defined as tonnes of CO2₂ equivalent 
per unit of product output. Entities that outperform their 
assigned targets will be eligible to earn CCCs, which can be 
traded on power exchanges. Conversely, entities falling short 
of their targets will be required to purchase and surrender 
equivalent CCCs to achieve compliance. The scheme is jointly 
administered by the Ministry of Power, MoEFCC, and the 
Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), with the Central Electricity 
Regulatory Commission (CERC) providing regulatory oversight. 
In January 2026, emission‑intensity targets were notified 
for seven energy‑intensive sectors - Aluminium, Cement, 
Chlor‑Alkali, Pulp & Paper, Petroleum Refining, Petrochemicals, 
and Textiles -covering approximately 490 entities with legally 
binding obligations for FY’26 and FY’27, using FY’24 as the 
baseline year. The baseline emission‑intensity target for FY’24 
was 480.25 tCO2e per tonne of equivalent product, while the 
cumulative emission target for FY’26 was reduced to 476.57 
tCO2e per tonne, reflecting India’s progressive decarbonization 
trajectory. 
Offsets are generated through accredited renewable energy, 
energy efficiency, and afforestation projects, validated under 
the supervision of the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) and 
aligned with Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement. Under the offset 
mechanism BEE has approved 10 sectors and 12 methodologies 
for buying

and selling CCCs on power exchanges which will 
increase the trading of such CCCs.
With the first compliance period now underway, obligated 
entities were required to submit their action plans to BEE by 
April 2026, followed by verified MRV reporting for FY’26 by July 
2026. CCC trading on the designated exchange is expected to 
formally open by October 2026, marking the beginning of active 
price discovery in India’s carbon market.

RISKS AND COMPLIANCES
Several risks can impact the achievement of IEX’s business 
objectives. Being present in a competitive and regulated 
environment, IEX is exposed to various risks such as financial, 
regulatory, information technology, cyber security, legal and 
market risk, among others. Our focused risk management 
approach seeks to minimise the adverse impact of these 
risks on our business and enables us to leverage market 
opportunities. Our well-defined enterprise risk management 
framework provides long-term competitive advantage through 
an established process involving risk identification, assessment, 
mitigation, measurement, monitoring and reporting which leads 
to transparent, smooth and seamless functioning. The risk 
management framework adopted by the Company is guided by 
ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management Guide

lines.
The focus of the risk management framework is primarily 
to mitigate perceived risks in the current structure of market 
dynamics that may affect the business.
IEX HAS CLASSIFIED FOUR TYPES OF MAJOR 
RISKS:
Regulatory Risks: These are risks which arise out of policy 
and regulatory changes related to the functioning of the power 
market and competitive landscape which can affect the long-
term functioning of the exchange and has an impact on the 
transaction volumes at the exchange.
Strategic Risks: These are risks which are internal or external 
in nature and are mostly related to the changing market 
scenario and developments in the value chain of generation, 
transmission & distribution, entry of new players, technological 
disruptions, etc. that may disrupt the strategic decisions taken 
to meet the objectives.
Operational Risks: These are risks which arise due to internal 
factors that can have a direct or indirect effect on internal 
policies, business processes, systems and our people in 
support functions, and thereby have the potential to impact our 
core business and values. Operational risks are mainly related 
to regulatory compliances as per Central Electricity Regulatory 
Commission’s Power Market Regulations and relevant orders, 
and risks related to finance, market operations etc., which may 
include the following:
• Technology related risk such as software failures, system 
downtime, or inadequate IT infrastructure.
• Market risk arising out of trading activities.
• Investment related risks such as fall in the value of investments, 
concentration of investment portfolio etc.
• Credit risk covering margin account maintenance leading to 
payment, security management and collateral management.
• Sustainability Risks (specifically Environmental Social and 
Governance (ESG) risks).
Cyber Security Risks: These are risks which are related to 
exposure or loss of data resulting from a cyber-attack or data 
breach on the organisation. It involves iden

tifying potential 
threats and vulnerabilities in your organisation’s digital 
systems and networks. The risk is not only about the likelihood 
of a cyberattack but also the potential consequences, such as 
financial loss, reputational damage, or operational disruption.
REGULATORY RISKS
Power markets are continuously evolving with several new 
policies and regulations notified from time to time to make the 
market deeper, more participative and transparent. The Central 
Electricity Regulatory Commission has implemented various 
regulations namely, Grid Code, GNA Regulation, Transmission 
Sharing Regulations, Ancillary Regulations, DSM Regulations 
etc. which have a bearing on the functioning of the power 
market. One of the key regulatory aspects which has direct 
bearing on the Exchange is Market Coupling. 
CERC vide its order dated 06 February 2024, directed Grid India 
to carry out pilot study to assess the impact of market coupling. 
As per the Grid India report, increase in economic surplus was 
0.3% which is insignificant. Based on the submissions made 
by Grid-India, CERC, vide its order dated 23 July 2025, decided 
to initiate the process for implementing market coupling of the 
Day-Ahead Market (DAM) and directed staff of commission 
to frame procedure and regulation for the implementation of 
same.
As per the order, with respect to the Real-Time Market (RTM), 
given the shorter time for bid submission and running the 
market clearing engine, the decision to implement the coupling 
of Real-Time Market (RTM) of the power exchanges shall be 
considered at a later stage after gaining operational experience 
from the coupling of DAM. Additionally, the feasibility of coupling 
the Term-Ahead Market (including Contingency Contracts) of 
the power exchanges shall be examined through a shadow 
pilot.
